paragraphs.text: [PROLOGUE.]

[In former times the ancients, out of their zeal for wisdom, never ceased to search out and inquire diligently into what events, and of what kind, had befallen provinces, places or regions, whether for good or ill. On these subjects and in these places they sharpened the pen of their talent, and offered to those who did not know history the fragrant flowers of their learning, served from their baskets as a free gift. They took pains that what had perhaps been done in one part should by no means remain wholly hidden.

But they, puffed up with the pride of worldly love, longed for the glory of their own self-exaltation to be spread far and wide with praise. Your venerable self, however, wishing to weave a history, makes inquiry with a similar fervour but from a different love. They wrote so that they might be praised in this world; you, so that you may appear glorious in the world to come and may say: "My soul shall be praised in the Lord; let the meek hear and be glad." You will be able to do as you wished, for you have received from heaven every good gift and every perfect gift, having been taught by so great a bishop, the blessed Diadochus, who deserves to be proclaimed with every kind of praise, and whose many writings of catholic doctrine stand out like shining stars. And it is enough for you to equal the teaching of your teacher, for it is enough for the disciple to be like his master.

I see in you another Timothy, taught in the sacred writings from the cradle of infancy, and also a Luke, a physician by profession and disciple of the apostle Paul, who stood out among others as eminent and ready in the teaching of the Gentiles. For my part, bowing the neck of obedience to the command of the one who bids me,

I will try to set out, step by step and briefly, what took place in the regions of Africa while the Arians raged. Like a rustic labourer with weary arms I shall gather gold from hidden caves, and I will not hesitate to hand over the ore, still dirty and mixed with dross, to the craftsman, to be assayed by the judgment of the fire, for he is able to stamp it into minted coins.]
BOOK ONE.

(I, 1) It is now, as is well known, the sixtieth year since that cruel and savage people, the Vandal race, reached the borders of wretched Africa. They crossed over easily by the narrow strait where this great, wide sea, lying between Spain and Africa, narrows to a channel only twelve miles across.

When the whole host had crossed, Gaiseric their leader cunningly decided to make his people's reputation terrifying, and at once ordered the entire multitude to be counted, down to those the womb had brought into the light that very day. All who were found, old men, young men, small children, slaves and masters, numbered eighty thousand. Once this figure was spread abroad, those who do not know the truth still reckon it to this day as the number of their fighting men, though that force is now small and weak.

They found a peaceful and quiet province, the beauty of a whole land in flower, and fell upon it on every side with their wicked bands. They laid it waste and plundered it, wiping everything out with fire and slaughter. They did not even spare the fruit trees, so that those who had hidden in mountain caves, on steep crags or in any remote place might not live off that food once they had passed. Raging with such cruelty again and again, they left no place untouched by their infection.

They raged most wickedly against the churches and the basilicas of the saints, the cemeteries and the monasteries, so that they burned houses of prayer with greater fires than they burned cities and towns. Wherever they happened to find the doors of a holy building shut, they vied with one another to hack a way in with axes, so that it could rightly be said then: "As in a forest of trees they hewed down its doors with axes; with hatchet and adze they brought it down. They set your sanctuary on fire; they defiled the dwelling place of your name on the ground."

(I, 2) How many eminent bishops and noble priests were then put to death by them with various kinds of torture, to make them hand over any gold or silver they had, whether their own or the church's! And when, under the pressure of torture, they readily gave up what there was, the Vandals pressed those who had handed it over with cruel torments once again, claiming that they had offered only part and not the whole; and the more that was given, the more they believed a man had.

Some they forced open the mouths of with stakes and bars and crammed stinking filth down their throats to make them confess where their money was. Some they tortured by twisting bowstrings around their foreheads and shins until the cords groaned. Often they mercilessly forced sea water on them, and on others vinegar, olive dregs, fish sauce and many other cruel things, putting them to their mouths as if they were wineskins to be filled. Neither the weaker sex, nor regard for noble birth, nor reverence for the priesthood softened their cruel hearts; on the contrary, their fury grew all the more where they saw the honour of rank.

I cannot tell how many priests and how many distinguished men they loaded with huge burdens as if they were camels or other kinds of beasts of burden, driving them along with iron goads; and some of them breathed their last miserably beneath their loads. The ripeness of age and venerable grey hair that had whitened the head like white wool won no mercy from these intruders. Indeed, barbarian fury even snatched little ones from their mothers' breasts and dashed innocent infants to the ground. Others they held by the feet, one on each side, and tore apart from the natural opening right up to the crown of the head. Then indeed captive Zion might have sung: "The enemy said he would burn my borders, kill my infants and dash my little ones to the ground."

(I, 3) In some buildings, great halls or houses, where fire had less effect, they utterly destroyed the roofs and levelled the beautiful walls to the ground, so that now the ancient beauty of the cities does not even show that it ever existed. Very many cities are inhabited by few people or none at all. Even today whatever survives is being continually laid waste: at Carthage, for example, they utterly destroyed the Odeon, the theatre, the temple of Memory and the street they called the Street of Caelestis.

To speak of what matters most: the great basilica where the bodies of the holy martyrs Perpetua and Felicity are buried, the basilica of Celerina, that of the Scillitans, and others which they did not destroy, they handed over to their own religion by tyrannical licence. Wherever there seemed to be fortified places which the barbarians' hostile fury could not take by storm, they gathered countless crowds around the walls and put them to the sword with savage blades, so that, by means of the rotting corpses, they might kill with the stench of decaying bodies those they could not reach because the walls kept them off.

Who could recount how many priests, and how great a number, were then tortured by them? It was then that the venerable Pampinianus, bishop of our own city, was burned all over his body with plates of red-hot iron. Likewise Mansuetus of Urusi was burned at the Fornitan Gate. At that time the city of Hippo Regius was besieged, which was governed as bishop by the blessed Augustine, worthy of all praise, the author of many books.

Then the river of eloquence that had flowed abundantly through all the fields of the church was dried up by fear itself, and the sweetness so sweetly poured out was turned into the bitterness of wormwood, so that David's words fitted well: "While the sinner stood against me, I was dumb and humbled, and kept silent even from good things." By that time he had already written two hundred and thirty-two books, not counting countless letters, his exposition of the whole Psalter and of the Gospels, and his sermons to the people, which the Greeks call homilies, whose number it is quite impossible to determine.

(I, 4) Why say more? After these savage and insane impieties, Gaiseric took and entered the very great city of Carthage itself, and reduced its ancient, freeborn and noble liberty to slavery; he also took captive no small number of the city's senators. Then he issued a decree that everyone was to hand over whatever gold, silver, jewels and costly garments he had; and so, by this device, the plunderer quickly carried off the wealth handed down from grandfathers and fathers.

He also arranged the provinces one by one. He kept Byzacena, Abaritana and Gaetulia and part of Numidia for himself, while he divided Zeugitana, the proconsular province, among his army by lot as an inheritance. Valentinian, who was still emperor, defended the remaining provinces, though they had already been ravaged. After Valentinian's death Gaiseric took possession of the whole circuit of Africa, and also, with his usual arrogance, held the great islands of Sardinia, Sicily, Corsica, Ebusus, Majorca, Minorca and many others.

One of these, Sicily, he later granted to Odoacer, king of Italy, on terms of tribute; from it Odoacer paid them tribute at fixed times as to his overlords, though they kept a part of it for themselves. Moreover, he did not hesitate at all to order the Vandals to drive the bishops and noble laymen out of their churches and homes, stripped of everything; and if, when given the choice, they were slow to leave, they were to remain slaves for ever. This was in fact done to very many. For we know of many bishops and laymen, distinguished and honoured men, who are slaves of the Vandals.

(I, 5) Then he ordered the bishop of that city, that is, of Carthage, a man known to God and men, named Quodvultdeus, together with a great crowd of clergy, to be put aboard broken-down ships and driven out, naked and stripped of everything. The Lord in the mercy of his goodness deigned to bring them by a prosperous voyage to Naples, a city of Campania. He first wore down a multitude of senators and men of rank with cruel exile, and afterwards cast them out overseas. Once the bishop, as we have said, had been expelled along with his venerable clergy, he at once handed over to his own religion the church called Restituta, where the bishops had always resided, and took away all the churches within the city walls together with their riches.

He also seized whatever churches he pleased outside the wall, especially two fine and spacious ones of the holy martyr Cyprian, one where he shed his blood and the other where his body is buried, a place called Mappalia. Who could bear it, or recall it without tears, when he ordered the bodies of our dead to be carried to burial in silence, without the solemn singing of hymns? He went further and ordered that the part of the clergy which had remained should be sent into exile as a punishment.

While this was going on, the great bishops and distinguished men who still survived in the provinces he had divided among the Vandals resolved to approach the king to plead with him. When he had gone out, as was his custom, to the shore at Maxula, which is commonly called Ligula, they came to meet him as suppliants, having already lost their churches and their property, asking that they at least be allowed to live there, now that the Vandals ruled, in order to comfort the people of God.

He is known to have answered them through a messenger, in a furious voice: "I have resolved to leave no one of your name and race, and you dare to ask such things of us?" He wanted to drown them in the nearby sea that very hour, and would have done so had his own people not begged him at length not to. They withdrew, worn out with sadness and grief, and, since their churches had been taken away, began to celebrate the divine mysteries however and wherever they could. And as the kingdom continually grew in wealth, its arrogance began to spread all the more.

(I, 6) I shall relate something that happened at that very time. There was a certain count Sebastian, son-in-law of the famous count Boniface, shrewd in counsel and vigorous in war. Gaiseric found his advice indispensable, but feared his presence just as much. Wishing to do away with him, he looked for a pretext for his death in the matter of religion. The king decided to address Sebastian in the presence of his bishops and his household, and spoke as follows: "Sebastian, I know that you have sworn to stand faithfully by us, and your labours and vigilance show the truth of your oath. But so that your friendship may remain bound to us always and without break, our priests here present have decided that you should become a follower of the religion which both we and our people revere."

Sebastian, hitting on a remarkable answer, and one useful to many, replied shrewdly on the spot: "I ask, my lord king, that a loaf of the finest bread, made of pure white flour, be brought here now." Gaiseric, not realizing that Sebastian was about to win, ordered it brought at once. Taking the fine loaf in his hands, Sebastian spoke as follows: "This bread, to reach such splendid beauty and be thought fit for the royal table, had the filth of the bran shaken out of it; then the mass of fine flour was moistened and passed through water and fire. That is why it is fair to look at and sweet to eat.

In the same way I too was ground in the mill of the Catholic mother, purified like fine flour by the sieve of testing, moistened with the water of baptism and baked in the fire of the Holy Spirit. And as this bread came out of the oven, so I, by the working of the divine sacraments, with God as the craftsman, came up clean from the font. But let it be done, if you wish, as I propose. Let this bread be broken into pieces, soaked in water and kneaded again, and put into the oven: if it comes out better, I will do what you urge." When Gaiseric and all who were present heard this proposal, he was so tied up that he could not get free at all. Later he killed this warlike man on a pretext of another kind.

(I, 7) To return to where we digressed: he terrorized our people with savage decrees, so that they could not breathe freely among the Vandals and no place was granted them anywhere to pray or offer sacrifice as they groaned, so that the words of the prophet were then plainly fulfilled: "At this time there is no prince, or prophet, or leader, nor any place to sacrifice to your name." Various false accusations were also brought every day even against those priests who lived in the regions that paid tribute to the palace. If, for example, while admonishing God's people, as was customary, someone happened to mention Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Holofernes or anyone like them, he was charged with having said it about the king, and was at once driven into exile. This kind of persecution was carried on openly in some places and secretly in others, so that the name of the faithful might perish through such snares. For this reason, we know that a great many priests were banished at that time:

such as Urban of Girba; Crescens, metropolitan of the city of Aquae, who had a hundred and twenty bishops under him; Habetdeum of Teudalis; Eustratius of Sufes; two from Tripolitania, Vicis of Sabratha and Cresconius of Oea; and Felix, bishop of the city of Hadrumetum, because he had taken in a certain John, a monk from overseas; and many others too, whom it would take long to list. Yet when death came to them in exile, others were not allowed to be ordained for their cities. Meanwhile, however, the people of God stood firm in the faith, and like swarms of bees building their waxen dwellings, they grew and were strengthened with the honeycombs of faith, so that the saying was fulfilled: "The more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong."

(I, 8) After this, at the request of the emperor Valentinian, it came about that after a long silence of desolation a bishop named Deogratias was ordained for the church of Carthage. If anyone tried to run through, bit by bit, the things the Lord did through him, his words would give out before he could recount any of it. After he had been installed as bishop, it came about, under the weight of sins, that in the fifteenth year of his reign Gaiseric captured Rome, that once most noble and famous city; and from there he carried off at once the riches of many kings together with their peoples.

When this multitude of captives reached the African shore, the Vandals and Moors divided up the huge number of people, and, as is the barbarians' way, husbands were separated from wives and children from parents. At once that man, full of God and dear to him, set about selling all the gold and silver vessels used in the liturgy to free free people from barbarian slavery, so that marriages might remain intact and children be returned to their parents. And because no places were large enough to hold so great a multitude, he set aside two well-known and spacious basilicas, the Basilica of Faustus and the Basilica Novarum, furnished with beds and bedding, and decided each day how much each person should receive according to need.

Because many had been afflicted by their unfamiliarity with sea travel and the cruelty of captivity, there was no small number of sick among them. That blessed bishop, like a devoted nurse, went round them constantly with doctors, with food following behind, so that once a person's pulse had been examined, whatever each needed might be given in his presence. Not even at night did he rest from this work of mercy, but hurried from bed to bed, asking how each was faring. He had so completely given himself to this labour that he spared neither his weary limbs nor his already frail old age.

The Arians, inflamed with envy at this, often tried to kill him by a great many tricks. I believe the Lord saw this clearly and wished to free his sparrow quickly from the hands of the hawks. The captives in the city mourned his death so deeply that they thought they were being handed over to the barbarians more truly when he went to heaven. He had held the office of bishop for three years. The people, intent on him out of love and longing, might have carried off the limbs of his worthy body, had he not been buried, by a prudent plan, while the multitude's attention was diverted and without their knowing.

(I, 9) Since one must not always keep silent about the impieties of the heretics, and there can be no shame in what serves to praise the one who suffers, the man who had once ordained that bishop, named Thomas, was often hard pressed by their various plots, and on one occasion they flogged the venerable old man across the shoulders in public view. He counted this not as a disgrace but as the reward of his glory, and rejoiced in the Lord.

After that it came about that, following the death of the bishop of Carthage, he forbade bishops to be ordained in Zeugitana, the proconsular province, where their number was one hundred and sixty-four. That number gradually dwindled, and now, if even these survive, there appear to be only three: Vincent of Gigi; Paul of Sinnar, truly a Paul in merit as in name; and another, Quintianus, who, fleeing the persecution, now lives as an exile at Edessa, a city of Macedonia.

(I, 10) There are also known to have been a great many martyrdoms, and a huge multitude of confessors, some of which I shall try to tell. There were at that time slaves of a certain Vandal (this Vandal was one of those they call millenarii, commanders of a thousand): Martinian, Saturian and their two brothers. There was also a fellow slave of theirs, an outstanding handmaid of Christ named Maxima, beautiful in body and in heart alike. Because Martinian was an armourer and was well liked by his master, and Maxima ran the whole household, the Vandal thought he would make these servants more loyal to him by joining Martinian and Maxima in marriage.

Martinian, like worldly young men, desired the marriage, but Maxima, already consecrated to God, refused human nuptials. When the time came for them to retire to the private quiet of the bedchamber, and Martinian, not knowing what God had decreed for him, wished with a husband's confidence to lie with her as his wife, the handmaid of Christ answered him aloud: "Brother Martinian, I have dedicated the members of my body to Christ, and I cannot enter into a human marriage, since I already have a true, heavenly bridegroom. But I will give you some advice: if you wish, you too can bring it about for yourself, while you may, to take delight in serving him whom I have longed to wed."

So it came about, by the Lord's providence, that the young man, by obeying the virgin, also won his own soul. Without the Vandal knowing of this spiritual and secret exchange, Martinian, pierced to the heart and changed, persuaded his brothers too to share as brothers the treasure he had found. So, converted together with his three brothers, and with the girl of God accompanying them, they slipped away secretly by night and joined the monastery at Tabraca, which was then ruled by a noble shepherd named Andrew. She settled in a monastery of virgins not far away.

The barbarian, however, made inquiries and offered many rewards, and what had been done could not be kept hidden. Finding them now no longer his own property but Christ's, he threw the servants of God into chains and persecuted them with various tortures, trying not only to make them live together as man and wife, but, what is worse, to defile the adornment of their faith through the filth of rebaptism. This came to the notice of Gaiseric himself. The king decreed that the implacable brute should go on tormenting his slaves until they gave in to his will. He ordered stout clubs to be made like saws, branching like palm fronds with their stumps left on, so that when they struck the victims' backs they would not only break their bones, but the piercing spikes would stay lodged inside.

Though their blood flowed and their flesh was torn apart so that their insides were laid bare, on the following day, with Christ as their physician, they were always restored whole. This was done often and over a long time, and no trace of the wounds could be seen, since the Holy Spirit healed them each time. After this Maxima was confined in harsh imprisonment and stretched out on a cruel stake. Since servants of God visited her in great numbers, they all saw the strength of the huge timbers rot and give way. This miracle is celebrated by everyone's report, and the man responsible for the prison testified to us under oath that it happened so.

(I, 11) But when the Vandal refused to recognize the power of God, avenging wrath began to rage in his house. He himself died, and his children with him; all the best of his household and his animals perished as well, and his wife was left a widow, bereft of husband, children and property. She offered the servants of Christ as a gift to Sesaon, a kinsman of the king. He received them with great delight, as an offering made to him, but then, on account of the saints, a demon began to torment his children and household servants with various convulsions. That kinsman reported to the king in order everything that had happened. The king at once decreed that they should be banished and sent to a pagan king of the Moors named Capsur. But Maxima, the handmaid of Christ, he let go, confounded and defeated, to do as she wished; she still lives, a virgin, the mother of many virgins of God, and well known to us too. On arriving, the others were handed over to that king of the Moors, who lived in a part of the desert called Caprapicti.

When the disciples of Christ saw the many unlawful sacrilegious sacrifices among the pagans, they began by their preaching and their way of life to invite the barbarians to the knowledge of the Lord our God; and in this way they won a huge multitude of pagan barbarians for Christ the Lord, in a place where the name of Christian had never before been made known by anyone. Then they considered what should be done so that the field, now tilled and cleared of weeds by the plough of preaching, might receive the seed of the Gospel and be watered with the rain of holy baptism.

They sent envoys along the long roads of the desert. At last they reached a Roman city, and the bishop was asked to send a priest and ministers to the people who had come to believe. God's bishop gladly did what was asked: a church was built, a very great multitude of barbarians was baptized, and from wolves a fruitful flock of lambs was multiplied. Capsur reported this to Geiseric. Rising up in envy at the news, Geiseric ordered that the servants of God have their feet bound and be dragged together behind racing four-horse chariots through the thorny places of the forest until they died, so that, dragged back and forth, the bodies of the innocent would be torn by the prickly thorns of the bushes. He bound them in such a way [?] that they could watch one another's end.

As the untamed horses ran close beside each other and the Moors wailed, the martyrs could see one another, and in the brief space of that rush each of them bade the others farewell, saying: "Brother, pray for me. God has fulfilled our desire: this is how one reaches the kingdom of heaven." And so, praying and singing psalms, they gave up their holy souls while the angels rejoiced. There, to this very day, Jesus Christ our Lord has not ceased to work great miracles. For the late blessed Faustus, bishop of Buruni, testified to us that a certain blind woman had received her sight there while he himself was present.
(I, 12) After this Geiseric's anger blazed up against the church of God.

He sent a certain Proculus into the province of Zeugitana to force the Lord's priests to hand over all the sacred vessels and books. The crafty enemy meant first to strip them of their weapons, so that once they were unarmed he could take them captive more easily. When the priests cried out that they could not hand them over, his men plundered everything themselves with greedy hands, and, shameful to say, they made shirts and trousers for themselves out of the altar cloths. But this Proculus, who carried out the order, soon died a most disgraceful death, chewing his own tongue to pieces.

At that time Saint Valerian, bishop of the city of Abbensa, fought manfully not to hand over the divine sacraments. He was ordered to be driven out of the city alone, and it was decreed that no one should let him stay either in a house or on a farm. For a long time he lay on the public road under the open sky. He was more than sixty-nine years old, and at that time, unworthy as we were, we had the privilege of greeting him in that exile.

(I, 13) Once, when the Easter festival was being celebrated, our people at a place called Regia opened for themselves a church that had been shut, to honour the day of Easter. The Arians found out. At once one of their priests, named Anduit, gathered a band of armed men and set off in a rage to attack the innocent crowd. They burst in with drawn swords and seized their weapons; others climbed onto the roof and shot arrows through the church windows. At that moment, as the people of God listened and sang, a reader standing in the pulpit was singing the Alleluia chant. Just then he was struck in the throat by an arrow; the book fell from his hands, and then he himself fell dead.

Many others too are known to have been killed by arrows and javelins right on the steps of the altar. Those who were not cut down by the sword at the time were afterward worn down by tortures on the king's orders, and almost all of them were put to death, especially the older ones. In other places, as happened at Tunuzuda, Gales, Vicus Ammoniae and elsewhere, they burst in in a great frenzy at the very moment when the sacraments of God were being given to the people, scattered the body and blood of Christ on the floor, and trampled it with their filthy feet.

(I, 14) At that same time, at the urging of his bishops, Geiseric had ordered that only Arians should be appointed to the various offices in his own court and in those of his sons. Among others it came to our Armogast. Again and again, for a long time, they twisted twanging cords around his shins and tightened them around his forehead, the forehead on which Christ had fixed the banner of his cross, so that they left it wrinkled and even furrowed, [?] tearing and [?] bellowing. Yet as the saint looked up to heaven the cords snapped like spiders' threads. When the torturers saw that the sinew cords had broken, they kept bringing stronger cords, even ropes of hemp; but while he called on nothing except the name of Christ, they all came to nothing. And when he was hung head downward by one foot, everyone thought he looked as if he were asleep on a feather bed.

Since the tortures had no effect, Theoderic, the king's son, who was his master, ordered him to be beheaded. But he was stopped by his priest Jucundus, who said to him, "You can kill him with various hardships; but if you put him to the sword, the Romans will begin to proclaim him a martyr." So Theoderic sentenced him to dig ditches in the province of Byzacena. Later, as if to disgrace him further, he ordered him to be a herdsman of cows not far from Carthage, where everyone could see him.

Meanwhile, when the Lord revealed to him that the day of his falling asleep was near, he called for a certain Felix, a venerable Christian who was steward of the king's son's household and who revered Armogast as an apostle, and said to him: "The time of my departure has come. I beg you by the faith we both hold to be so good as to bury me under this carob tree; if you do not, you will have to answer for it to our Lord." It was not that he cared where or how his body was buried, but that what God had revealed to his servant might be shown.

Felix answered, "Far be it from us, venerable confessor! No, I will bury me you in one of the basilicas with the triumph and honour you deserve." The blessed Armogast replied, "No, you will do what I have said." Felix, afraid of grieving the man of God, sincerely promised to do what he had commanded. Within a very few days the companion of the good confession departed this life. Felix hurried to dig the grave he had been charged with under the tree. When the tangled roots and the hardness of the dry ground caused delay and toil, he was distressed that the saint's body would be buried late. At last, after cutting away the roots and digging much deeper into the earth, they saw a sarcophagus of the most splendid marble lying ready, such as perhaps no king had ever had.

(I, 15) Nor should I pass over a certain chief mime named Mascula. He was pressed with many snares to make him abandon the catholic faith, and later the king himself tried to win him over with flattering worldly talk, promising to heap great riches on him if he would lend a ready ear to his wishes. When he remained firm and unconquered, the king ordered him to undergo capital punishment. But the crafty king gave secret instructions: if at the moment the sword was brandished he was terrified of the blow, he should all the more be killed, so that he would not become a glorious martyr; but if he was seen to be steadfast in his confession, the sword was to be held back. And he, made strong by Christ's support, stood like an immovable pillar and returned a glorious confessor. Though the envious enemy refused to make him a martyr, he could not harm our confessor.
(I, 16) We also knew another man at that time, named Saturus.

He was a shining member of Christ's church and often rebuked the depravity of the Arians with catholic frankness. He was steward of Huneric's household. On the accusation of a certain deacon Marivad, whom the ill-starred Huneric held in special honour, he was summoned to become an Arian. Honours and great riches were promised if he did so, and dreadful punishments were made ready if he refused. The choice was put to him: if he did not obey the royal commands, then first, after an inquiry, he would lose his house and property, all his slaves and children would be sold, and his wife would be given in marriage to a camel driver before his very eyes.

But he, full of God, provoked the ungodly all the more, so that it might happen quickly. For this reason his wife, without her husband's knowledge, asked those carrying out the order for a reprieve. Then she came to her husband, another Eve taught by the counsel of the serpent. But he was no Adam, to touch the alluring fruit of the forbidden tree, for his name was not Needy but Saturus, "the Sated": he was sated with the abundance of God's house and had drunk from the torrent of his delights. The woman came to the place where her husband was praying alone, her clothes torn and her hair loose, her children with her, carrying in her arms a little girl who was still nursing. She threw the baby at the feet of her unsuspecting husband, and she herself clasped his knees in her arms, hissing with the voice of the dragon: "Have pity on me, my dearest, and on yourself as well; have pity on our children, whom you see here. Do not let them be subjected to slavery, when the lineage of our family has made them noble. Do not let me be subjected to an unworthy and shameful marriage while my husband is still alive, I who always used to boast among women of my age about my Saturus. God knows that you will be doing unwillingly what some have perhaps done willingly."

He answered her in the words of holy Job: "You speak like one of the foolish women. I would be afraid, woman, if the bitter sweetness of this life were all there is. You are serving the devil's scheme, wife. If you loved your husband, you would never drag your own husband toward the second death. Let them sell my children, take my wife, carry off my property: I will hold securely to the words of my Lord's promises: 'Whoever does not leave wife, children, fields or house cannot be my disciple.'" What more is there to say? The woman went away with her children, rebuffed; Saturus was strengthened for his crown. He was interrogated, stripped of everything, crushed with tortures, and sent away a beggar, and he was forbidden to appear in public. They took everything from him, but they could not take away the robe of his baptism.

(I, 17) After this Geiseric ordered the church of Carthage to be closed, and since there was no bishop, its priests and ministers were scattered and dispersed to various places of exile. It was reopened only with difficulty, at the request of the emperor Zeno conveyed through the patrician Severus; and so all of them returned from exile. As for what he did in Spain, Italy, Dalmatia, Campania, Calabria, Apulia, Sicily, Sardinia, Bruttium, Lucania, Old Epirus and Greece, those who suffered there will better tell its pitiful and lamentable story. But let this be the end of our persecution as carried out by Geiseric, as cruel as it was grand. He reigned for thirty-seven years and three months.
BOOK TWO.

(II, 1) So when Geiseric died, his elder son Huneric succeeded his father. At the beginning of his reign, as is the cunning way of barbarians, he began to act more mildly and with more restraint, especially towards our religion. Where under King Geiseric it had earlier been forbidden to hold spiritual assemblies, the people now flocked together to their gatherings. And to show himself religious, he ordered a careful search for the Manichaean heretics. Many of them he burned, and a great many he sold off overseas by ship. He found that nearly all these Manichaeans belonged to his own religion, especially priests and deacons of the Arian heresy, and his shame at this made him rage against them all the more.

Among them was found one of their monks, named Clementianus, who had written on his thigh: "A Manichaean, disciple of Christ Jesus." For this reason the tyrant we have mentioned seemed all the more praiseworthy. He displeased in one thing only: he gaped greedily after wealth with an insatiable desire, and he burdened the provinces of his kingdom with all kinds of false charges and levies, so that it could be said of him above all: "A king in want of revenue is a great oppressor." However, at the request of the emperor Zeno and of Placidia, the widow of Olybrius, he gave permission for the church of Carthage to ordain for itself whatever bishop it wished, for it had been deprived of such an ornament for twenty-four years.

(II, 2) So he now sent the illustrious Alexander to the church with a message to this effect: that in his presence the Catholic people should ask for a worthy bishop for themselves. Through his notary, named Vitarit, he also sent an edict to be read publicly, which ran as follows:

"Our lord has ordered us to say this to you. Since the emperor Zeno and the most noble Placidia have written through Alexander, a man of illustrious rank, asking that the church of Carthage should have a bishop of your own religion, he has ordered that this be done. He has written back to them, and has ordered the envoys they sent to be told, that, as they requested, you may ordain for yourselves whatever bishop you wish, on this condition: that by the emperor's command the bishops of our religion in Constantinople and throughout the other provinces of the East, who are our bishops, shall have free choice to preach to the people in their churches in whatever languages they wish and to practise the Christian law, just as you here and in the other churches established in the African provinces have free choice to celebrate masses and preach in your churches, and to do whatever belongs to your law as you wish. For if this is not observed towards them, then the bishop who has been ordained and his clergy, and also the other bishops with their clergy in the African provinces, are ordered to be sent among the Moors."

When this edict was read to the whole church in our presence on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, we began to groan and murmur among ourselves, for we saw that the wicked were plotting their tricks and a persecution was being prepared. It is on record that we said to the envoy: "If that is how it is, then with such dangerous conditions attached this church has no wish to have a bishop. Christ governs it, and he has always deigned to govern it." But the envoy took no notice of this plea. At the same time the people, insisting that the ordination should take place then and there, blazed up like fire; their clamour was unbearable, and nothing could calm it.

(II, 3) And so Eugenius, a holy man and pleasing to God, was ordained bishop, and great rejoicing arose, and the joy of the church of God was complete. The Catholic multitude exulted that under barbarian rule the episcopate had been restored by this ordination; indeed a very large number of young men and girls, rejoicing together, declared that they had never seen a bishop sitting on his throne. And that man of God, the bishop Eugenius, by a life full of good works began to be held venerable and reverend even by those outside, and became so dear to everyone that all would gladly have laid down their lives for him, had it been lawful.

The Lord also deigned to give such alms through him that it seems incredible he could spend so much, when it is known that the church, with the barbarians holding everything, did not have the means of a single coin. Should anyone attempt to describe the humility, charity and devotion that God had granted him, he would be unable to do it. It is certain that money never stayed with him, unless perhaps it was offered at the hour when the sun, finishing its daily course, was giving way and yielding its place to the darkness of night. He kept only as much as would be enough for a day, not as much as greed would have wanted, and our God gave him great and ever greater gifts day after day.

But as his fame became widespread and well known, the bishops of the Arians began to be tormented by bitter envy, and they harassed him with daily false accusations, Cyrila above all. Why say more? They urged the king that he should by no means sit on his throne or preach his customary sermon to the people of God, and further that he should forbid entry to any men or women he saw coming into the church in barbarian dress. He answered as was fitting: "The house of God is open to all; no one may drive away those who enter." This was especially so because a great multitude of our Catholics went about in their dress, since they served in the royal household.

(II, 4) When the king received such an answer from the man of God, he had torturers posted at the doors of the church. Whenever they saw a woman or a man walking in the dress of their own people, they would at once throw small toothed stakes onto their heads, twist their hair around them, and pull with great violence, tearing off the whole scalp along with the hair. Some lost their eyes on the spot while this was being done; others died from the pain itself. The women, after this punishment, their heads stripped of skin, were led through the streets with a herald going before them, to be put on display to the whole city. Those who suffered this counted it rather as the greatest gain. We knew a great many of them, and we do not know of any one of them who, even under the pressure of these torments, turned aside from the right path.

When he could not break down the wall of faith in this way, he decided that men of our religion who held posts at his court should receive neither their rations nor their usual pay. He went further and wore them down with farm labour. He sent freeborn men, and very delicate ones at that, to the plain of Utica, to cut the stalks of the harvest under the blazing heat of the sun. All of them went there with joy and rejoiced in the Lord.

In their company was a man with a withered hand, which for very many years had been of no use to him. Though he truthfully pleaded that he could not work, he was ordered all the more violently to go. But when they came to the place and all of them groaned in prayer for him above all, by God's mercy the confessor's withered hand was restored to health. From this point the persecution of Huneric, the beginning of our sorrows and our birth pangs, took its start.

(II, 5) Now he who had for some time shown himself gentle to all, wishing to secure the kingdom for his sons after his death, which did not come to pass, began cruelly to hunt down his brother Theoderic and his sons, and likewise the sons of his brother Gento. He would have spared none of them, had not death taken away from him the fulfilment of his desire. First, knowing that his brother Theoderic's wife was shrewd, and fearing, I believe, that she might arm her husband or her elder son, who seemed prudent and wise, with sharper counsels against the tyrant, he had a charge brought against her and ordered her to be put to the sword.

Afterwards that son too was killed, a man of great learning, to whom, according to Geiseric's settlement, the kingdom was owed above all the grandsons because he was the eldest of them all. The king was then inflamed to commit something still more cruel. Before the assembled crowd, in the middle of the city, in front of the steps of the New [?] Square, he ordered a bishop of his own religion named Jucundus, whom they called patriarch, to be burned alive, because he was a great favourite in the household of Theoderic, the king's brother, and through his support that household might have obtained the kingdom. In this impious crime we foresaw the evil that was coming upon us, and we said to one another: "If this man has been so cruel to his own bishop, when will he spare our religion or us?"

Then he sent Godagis, the elder son of Gento, together with his wife, into cruel exile, without the comfort of a single slave or maidservant. His brother Theoderic, after the killing of his wife and son, he likewise exiled, naked and destitute. After Theoderic's death he drove away to a distant place the little son who survived him and his two grown daughters, set on donkeys to torment them. He also harassed a great many counts and nobles of his own people with false charges, on the ground that they favoured his brother; some he burned, others he had their throats cut. In this he imitated his father Geiseric, who had a weight of stones tied to his own brother's wife and threw her into the Ampsaga, the famous river of Cirta, and after the mother's murder killed her sons as well.

Moreover, his father Geiseric on his deathbed had commended many people to him under oath; but he, forgetful of his word and violating his oath, put them to death with various punishments and by fire. Heldica, for instance, whom his father had made chief officer of the kingdom, by then an old man full of years, he beheaded in disgrace, and he burned Heldica's wife, along with another woman named Teucharia, in the middle of the city. He ordered their bodies to be dragged through the streets and squares, and they lay there all day; only at evening, at the request of his bishops, did he reluctantly allow them to be buried. Heldica's brother Gamuth he could not kill, because he had fled to their church; but he shut him up in a filthy place of latrines and made him live there for a long time. Afterwards

he condemned him, together with a goatherd and a peasant, to dig trenches for planting vines. Twelve times a year, that is, every month, he had them torn with cruel whips, allowing them barely a little water and coarse bread. They endured this for five years or more. These punishments might have won them an eternal reward if they had been Catholics and had borne them for the sake of their faith. But we could not pass this over in silence, so as not to keep quiet about the king's impiety even towards his own people. Not only did he burn his own bishop Jucundus, as we showed above, but he also burned a great many of his own priests and deacons, that is, Arians, and handed others over to the beasts.

(II, 6) So when he had quickly cut off all those he feared and had made secure for himself, as he thought, a kingdom that was to be short and perishable, he was free of cares and safe on every side, and roaring like a lion he turned all the weapons of his fury to persecuting the Catholic Church. Before the storm of persecution, however, the coming evil had been foretold by many visions and signs.

For about two years before it happened, a certain man saw the Basilica of Faustus shining in its usual splendour, gleaming with candles and glowing with hangings, curtains and lamps. And while he was rejoicing in the brightness of such splendour, suddenly, he said, the glow of that lovely light went out; darkness followed, and a stench offensive to the nostrils arose; and all that crowd of the blessed was driven outside by certain Ethiopians. He grieved continually at this, because he never saw the church restored to its former brightness. He told this vision to the holy Eugenius in our presence. A certain priest also saw the same Basilica of Faustus packed with crowds of countless people, and shortly afterwards emptied and filled with a multitude of pigs and goats.

Again, another man saw a threshing floor of wheat ready for winnowing, the grain not yet separated from the chaff by the winnower's judgement. And while he marvelled at the size of the huge heap, mixed though it was, suddenly a whirlwind came with a storm, announcing its arrival with a roaring blast and rising dust; and at its onset all the chaff flew off entirely, while the grain remained. After this came a tall man with a radiant face, shining in bright clothing, and he began to clean the grain, throwing out the empty and shrivelled kernels that were unfit for fine flour. He examined it for a long time, and that great heap, though now proved, he brought down to a small pile.

Again, another said: "A very tall man stood on the mountain called Ziquensis and cried out to the right and to the left: 'Move away, move away!'" Another saw, while the sky roared and was in turmoil, sulphurous clouds which began to hurl down huge stones; when these stones fell to the ground, they caught fire all the more and burned with greater flames, and entering the inner rooms of houses they burned whomever they found. But the man who saw it said that, since he had hidden himself in a certain chamber, by God's mercy the flame could not reach him. I think this was so that the prophetic word might be fulfilled: "Shut your door and hide yourself for a little while, until the wrath of God passes by."

The venerable bishop Paul also saw a tree reaching up to the heavens with flowering branches, which by its spreading shaded almost the whole of Africa. And while everyone was rejoicing at its size and beauty, suddenly, he said, a violent donkey came along and, rubbing its neck against the trunk at its roots, threw that marvellous tree to the ground with a great crash.

And Quintianus, the honourable bishop, saw himself standing on a mountain, from which he looked out on a countless flock of his sheep; and in the middle of the flock were two cauldrons boiling furiously. Slaughterers of the sheep were there, and they plunged the sheep's flesh into the boiling cauldrons; and as this went on, that whole great flock was consumed. I think, then, that those two cauldrons were the two cities of Sicca Veneria and Lares, where the multitude was first gathered and where the burning began; or else King Huneric and his bishop Cyrila. But of the many visions, since brevity must be considered, let it be enough to have told these.

(II, 7) What more? First the tyrant decreed by a terrible order that no one should serve in his palace or hold public office unless he had made himself an Arian. A huge number of them, strong and unconquered, gave up their earthly service so as not to lose their faith; these he afterwards drove from their homes, stripped of all their property, and banished to the islands of Sicily and Sardinia. At one point he hastened to decree throughout all Africa that the treasury should claim for him the property of our bishops when they died, and that whoever was able to succeed a deceased bishop should not be ordained until he had paid five hundred solidi to the royal treasury.

But as soon as the devil tried to put up this building, Christ deigned to pull it down. The king's own household urged him, saying: "If your command enforces this, our bishops settled in Thrace and other regions will begin to suffer worse." Then he ordered the consecrated virgins to be gathered, and sent Vandals with midwives of their own people to inspect and handle, against all the laws of modesty, the private parts of their chastity, where neither their mothers nor any of the matrons were present. They tortured them by hanging them up cruelly, tying huge weights to their feet, and they applied red-hot plates of iron to their backs, bellies, breasts and sides.

During the tortures they were told: "Say that the bishops and your clergy sleep with you." We know that very many of them died at that time from the harshness of the torments; the others who survived were left bent over, their skin shrivelled. For the king was striving to find a path by which he might launch a public persecution, as indeed he did. Yet though he did this, he could find no way at all to stain the Church of Christ.

(II, 8) With what rivers of tears shall I go on, now that I come to the time when he sent bishops, priests, deacons and other members of the Church, four thousand nine hundred and sixty-six in all, into exile in the desert? Among them were a great many with gout, and others who through the years of age had been deprived of the light of this world. Among their number was the blessed Felix, bishop of Abbir, who had already been a bishop for forty-four [?] years; struck by paralysis, he could neither feel anything nor speak at all.

Being especially concerned for him, since he could not be carried on a beast, we suggested that his people should petition the king to order that he at least remain in Carthage, since he would soon die and could in no way be taken into exile. The tyrant is reported to have said in a rage: "If he cannot sit on an animal, let wild oxen be yoked, to drag him along tied with ropes to where I have ordered." So we carried him the whole way, tied crosswise over a mule like a log of wood.

(II, 9) They were all gathered in the cities of Sicca and Lares, so that the Moors could meet them there and take those handed over to them into the desert. Then two counts arrived and with damnable cunning began to work on the confessors of God with smooth words. "What do you think you are doing," they said, "being so stubborn and refusing to obey the commands of our lord, when you could be held in honour in the king's sight if you hurried to do his will?" At once the confessors shouted out with a mighty cry: "We are Christians, we are Catholics, we confess the Trinity, one inviolable God!" They were then shut up in a harsher prison, though one still roomy enough that we were allowed to go in, speak a word of exhortation to the brothers, and celebrate the divine mysteries.

There were also a great many little children there, whose mothers followed them with a mother's love, some rejoicing, others trying to hold them back. Some rejoiced that they had given birth to martyrs; others tried to call them back from confessing the faith, to die in the flood of rebaptism. Yet at that time no flattery overcame anyone, and no fleshly affection bent anyone down to the ground. Indeed, it is a pleasure to tell briefly what a certain old woman did then.

As we were travelling along with the army of God, and as we happened to move on mostly at night because of the heat of the sun, we saw a poor woman carrying a sack and some clothes, holding a little child by the hand and comforting him with these words: "Run, my lord! Do you see how all the saints are going on, hurrying cheerfully to their crowns?" When we rebuked her, because it seemed improper for her, being a woman, to join the men or to keep company with the army of Christ, she answered: "Bless me, bless me, and pray for me and for this little grandson of mine, for, sinner though I am, I am the daughter of a former bishop of the city of Zurita." We said to her: "And why are you walking along in such a humble state, and for what reason are you seen to have come all this long way?" She replied: "I am going into exile with this little servant of yours, so that the enemy may not find him alone and call him back from the way of truth to death." At these words we were filled with tears and could say nothing, except that the will of God be done.

(II, 10) But the adversary, who perhaps was already saying, "I will divide the spoil, I will fill my soul, I will kill with my sword, my hand shall rule," could catch no one; so he searched out narrow and loathsome places in whose confined rooms he might cram the army of God. Then even the comfort of human visits was denied them; guards were posted at the doors, and they were grievously afflicted. The confessors of Christ were thrown on top of one another, packed so tightly, one upon another, like swarms of locusts, or, to put it more fittingly, like the most precious grains of wheat.

In this crush there was no room to withdraw to answer the needs of nature; under pressure of necessity they relieved themselves of excrement and urine right there, so that the stench and horror of it surpassed every kind of torment. On one occasion, after we had given large bribes to the Moors, we were secretly let in, with difficulty, while the Vandals slept. As we went in we began to sink up to our knees as though in a pool of mud, and we saw fulfilled then the word of Jeremiah: "Those who were brought up in scarlet have embraced their own dung." Why say more? With the Moors raising an uproar on every side, they were ordered to get ready for the journey to the place they had been sentenced to.

(II, 11) So they came out on the Lord's day, their clothes, faces and heads smeared with excrement, and though the Moors drove them on cruelly, they sang a hymn to the Lord with exultation: "This is the glory of all his saints." Present there at that time was the blessed prelate Cyprian, bishop of Unizibir, an outstanding comforter, who cherished each of them with tender, fatherly love, not without rivers of flowing tears. He was ready to lay down his life for his brothers and to give himself up willingly to such sufferings, if he were allowed; in that time of need he spent everything he had on his brothers in want. For he was seeking an opportunity to join the confessors, being himself a confessor in spirit and in courage. Afterwards, through many struggles and the squalor of prison, he went with exultation into the exile he longed for.

The roads and paths bear witness to how great were the crowds of people who came then from different regions and cities to see God's martyrs. The roads could not hold the throngs that came, so a countless crowd of the faithful ran together and came down over the mountaintops and tracks, carrying candles in their hands. They threw their little children at the martyrs' feet and cried out: “To whom are you leaving us wretches, as you go to your crowns? Who will baptize these little ones in the water of the everlasting font? Who will give us the gift of penance, and loose us from the chains of our sins by the pardon of reconciliation? For it was said to us: Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven. Who will bury us with the solemn prayers when we die? By whom will the customary rite of the divine sacrifice be performed? We would gladly go with you too, if it were allowed, so that no necessity would separate sons from their fathers in this way.”

Amid these cries and tears no one who might comfort them was allowed to go any further. Instead the crowd of confessors was forced to run, so that they would reach the hard lodging where a camp had been prepared for them. When the old men began to give out, and perhaps others too, even young men who had been delicately raised, they were driven on with spear points and stones to make them run. So, already flagging, they grew all the more exhausted.

(II, 12) Then the Moors were ordered to tie the feet of those who could not walk and drag them like the carcasses of dead animals over hard, rough, stony ground. There first their clothes and then each of their limbs were torn away. On the sharp blades of the rocks one man's head was crushed, another's sides were split open, and so they breathed out their spirits in the hands of those who dragged them. We could not count their number, because the crowd kept us back. Yet all along the public highway the humble graves of the saints cry out, their tombs speaking for them.

The rest, who were more able-bodied, reached the desert places. There they were settled and received barley to eat, like beasts of burden. It is said that there are so many venomous creatures and scorpions there that those who do not know the place would find it unbelievable, and that by their breath alone they can pour their poison even into people some distance away. They say that no one has ever survived a scorpion's sting. Yet we are told that up to the present time, with Christ defending them, their venomous fury has harmed none of his servants. While the exiles were being fed there on grains of barley, later even this was taken away from them, as if God, who rained down manna on the fathers, could not also feed those who had now been consigned to such an exile.

(II, 13) He planned fiercer measures against the church of God, so that, having cut off some of its limbs, he might tear the whole body apart and destroy it. On the day of the Lord's Ascension, in the presence of Reginus, the envoy of the emperor Zeno, he sent Bishop Eugenius an edict to be read in the middle of the church. It was written as follows, and he also sent it by swift post-horses to the whole of Africa.

“King Huneric of the Vandals and Alans to all the homoousian bishops. It is well known that your priests have been forbidden, not once but repeatedly, to hold assemblies in the lands allotted to the Vandals, lest they lead Christian souls astray by their seduction. Scorning this, very many of them have been found to have celebrated masses in the Vandal lands against the prohibition, claiming that they hold the whole rule of the Christian faith intact. And because we do not want there to be any scandal in the provinces granted to us by God, know therefore that by God's providence, with the consent of our holy bishops, we have decreed as follows. On the day of the Kalends of February next, setting aside every excuse of fear, you are all to come to Carthage, so that you may enter into debate with our venerable bishops about the principles of the faith, and may duly prove from the divine Scriptures the faith of the homoousians which you defend, so that it may be known whether you hold the faith intact. We have sent the text of this edict to all your fellow bishops throughout the whole of Africa. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the seventh year of Huneric.”

(II, 14) When those of us who were present learned of this and read it together, our hearts were crushed at once and our eyes grew dark. Then truly our feast days were turned into mourning and our songs into lamentation, for the wording of the edict revealed the fury of the persecution to come. This was especially clear where it said, “We do not want there to be any scandal in the provinces granted to us by God,” as if to say, “We do not want there to be Catholics in our provinces.” We discussed what should be done. No remedy could be found for the impending calamity, except that holy Eugenius should submit a reasoned petition, in case the barbarian's heart might be softened. It was written in these terms:

“Whenever the cause of the soul, of eternal life and of the Christian faith is under consideration, what is fitting must be put forward without fear, as the royal providence has promised. Recently the royal power deigned to give notice to my lowliness through the notary Vitarit. On account of our religion and faith, he rightly read out the king's order to us in the church in the presence of the clergy and people. From its wording we learned that a royal order had gone out likewise to all my fellow bishops, that they should come on an appointed day for a disputation about the faith. We replied that we had received this with reverence. My humility also suggested to the said notary that our brothers in all the lands overseas, who share one religion and communion with us, ought to be informed as well, since all everywhere are subject to his kingdom; above all because this is a cause that concerns the whole world, not the African provinces alone.

“And since I promised to offer a petition in a second reply, I rightly and humbly ask your magnificence to deign to bring my said petition to the ears of our lord, the most clement king, so that his clemency may graciously understand that, with God's help, we in no way decline or run from a disputation about the law, but that without the assent of the whole church we ought not to take up the cause of defending our faith alone. We ask that, in his great kindness and the justice of his wisdom, he deign to grant this. Given by Eugenius, bishop of the catholic church of Carthage.”

(II, 15) But when blessed Eugenius had offered this petition, the king, who had already conceived mischief, was driven to bring forth iniquity all the more grievously. He is said to have sent word to the holy man, Bishop Eugenius, through Obadus, the provost of his kingdom: “Subject the whole world to me, so that all the earth is brought under my power, and then, Eugenius, I will do what you say.” Blessed Eugenius answered as best he could: “What makes no sense ought not to have been said. It is as if a man were told to be carried through the air and fly, which is not in the nature of human beings. What I said was this: if the king's power wishes to learn our faith, which is the one true faith, let him send to his friends. I too will write to my brothers, so that my fellow bishops may come who can show you, together with us, the faith we hold in common; and especially the Roman church, which is the head of all the churches.”

To this Obadus said: “So you and my lord the king are equals?” Bishop Eugenius said: “I am not the king's equal. But I said: if he wishes to learn the true faith, let him write to his friends and ask them to send our catholic bishops, and I will write to my fellow bishops, because the whole catholic church has one cause.” Eugenius did this not because Africa lacked men who could refute the objections of our adversaries, but so that bishops would come who, being outside the Vandals' rule, would have greater confidence to speak freely, and who would at the same time make known to all lands and peoples the false charges by which we were oppressed.

(II, 16) But he who was weaving his schemes would not listen to reason. He used one pretext after another to harass with various persecutions any bishops he had heard were learned. He had already sent Secundianus, bishop of Vibiana, into exile after having him beaten with a hundred and fifty blows of the club, and also Praesidius of Sufetula, a very sharp-minded man. At that time he also had the venerable Mansuetus, Germanus, Fusculus and many others beaten.

While this was going on, he ordered that no one of their religion should share a table with people of ours, nor eat with Catholics at all. This brought no benefit to them, but it brought us the greatest gain. For if their talk, as the apostle says, is apt to spread like a cancer, how much more could a shared table of food defile, since the same apostle says not even to eat with the wicked.

(II, 17) When the fire of persecution was already kindled and the flame of the hostile king was blazing everywhere, our God showed a miracle through his faithful servant Eugenius which I must not pass over. In that same city, Carthage, there was a blind citizen, very well known in the city, named Felix. The Lord visited him, and in a vision at night (for the day of the Epiphany was dawning) he was told: “Get up, go to my servant Bishop Eugenius and tell him that I have sent you to him. At the hour when he blesses the font, so that those coming to the faith may be baptized, he will touch your eyes. They will be opened, and you will see the light.”

Though warned by this visitation, the blind man thought he was being deceived by a dream, as often happens, and would not get up. But when he sank back into sleep, he was urged in the same way to go to Eugenius. Again he ignored it, and a third time he was rebuked urgently and sternly. He woke the boy who used to give him his hand, and went with all speed to the Basilica of Faustus. When he arrived, he prayed with many tears and asked a deacon named Peregrinus to announce him to the bishop, saying that he had something like a secret to tell him.

When the bishop heard this, he ordered the man to be brought in. By now, for the solemnity of the feast, the night hymns were resounding through the whole church as the people sang. The blind man told the bishop the course of his visitation and said to him: “I will not let you go unless you give me back my eyes, as the Lord has commanded you.” Holy Eugenius said to him: “Leave me, brother. I am a sinner and unworthy, guiltier than all other men, seeing that I have been kept alive even into these times.”

But he held on to his knees and said nothing except what he had already said: “Give me back my eyes, as you have been commanded.” Eugenius, considering his unabashed faith, and since time was pressing, went with him to the font, attended by the clergy. There he knelt down with great groaning, beating at heaven with his sobs, and blessed the rippling basin of the font. When he had finished his prayer and risen, he answered the blind man: “I have told you already, brother Felix, I am a sinful man. But may he who deigned to visit you grant it to you according to your faith and open your eyes.” At the same moment he marked his eyes with the sign of the cross, and at once the blind man received his sight, for the Lord restored it. Eugenius kept him there with him until everyone had been baptized, so that the people, roused by so great a miracle, would not crush the man who had received his sight.

Afterwards it was made known to the whole church. The man who had been blind went up to the altar with Eugenius, as is the custom, to make an offering to the Lord for his healing, and the bishop took it and placed it on the altar. The people broke into an uproar of joy that could not be stilled. At once a messenger went to the tyrant. Felix was seized and questioned about what had happened and how he had received his sight. He told them everything in order, and the Arian bishops said: “Eugenius did this by sorcery.” Overwhelmed with confusion, they could not cloud over the light, because Felix was known and recognized by the whole city. Yet they wanted to kill him if they could, just as the Jews longed to kill Lazarus after he was raised.

(II, 18) The slanderous day he had appointed, the Kalends of February, was now approaching. Bishops gathered not only from all of Africa but also from many islands, worn down by affliction and grief. For many days there was silence, until he had singled out from among them all the skilled and most learned men, to be put to death on trumped-up charges. One of that very company of teachers, a vigorous and most learned man named Laetus, he burned alive after a long time in the squalor of prison, thinking that by such an example he would strike fear into the rest and crush them.

At last they came to the contest of the disputation, at a place chosen by our adversaries. To avoid an uproar of shouting, so that the Arians could not say later that they had been overwhelmed by our numbers, our bishops chose ten of their own number to answer for all. Cyrila, with his attendants, set up a most arrogant throne for himself on a raised platform, while our men stood. Our bishops said: “A conference is always welcome where proud arrogance does not hold sway, but where people come together by common consent, so that, with judges deciding and the parties pleading their case, the truth may be recognized. Now who will be the judge, who the examiner, to confirm with the scales of justice what is rightly put forward, or refute what is wrongly assumed?”

When these and other things had been said, the king's notary replied: “The patriarch Cyrila has said [?].” Our men, detesting a title so arrogantly and unlawfully usurped, said: “Let it be read to us by whose grant Cyrila has taken this title for himself.” At that our adversaries raised a clamor and began to bring false charges. And because our men had asked that, if the wise multitude was not allowed to examine the case, it should at least be allowed to watch, all the sons of the catholic church who were present were ordered to be beaten with a hundred blows each. Then blessed Eugenius began to cry out: “May God see the violence we suffer; may he take note of the affliction we endure from our persecutors.”

Our men turned to Cyrila and said: “Set out what you propose.” Cyrila said: “I do not know Latin.” Our bishops said: “We know perfectly well that you have always spoken Latin. You ought not to make excuses now, especially since it was you who set this fire alight.” Seeing that the catholic bishops were better prepared for the contest, he avoided a hearing altogether with various quibbles. Our men had foreseen this beforehand and had written a booklet on the faith, composed with due propriety and thoroughness, saying: “If you wish to learn our faith, this is the truth we hold.”

(III, 1) By royal command we are ordered to give an account of the catholic faith that we hold. We therefore undertake, as far as our modest strength allows and relying on God's help, to set out briefly what we believe and preach. First, we recognize that we must explain the unity of substance of the Father and the Son, which the Greeks call homoousion. We profess the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in the unity of the Godhead in such a way that we acknowledge in faithful confession that the Father subsists in his own distinct person, that the Son likewise exists in his own person, and that the Holy Spirit retains what is proper to his person. We do not assert that the Father is the same as the Son, nor confess that the Son is the one who is the Father or the Holy Spirit, nor do we understand the Holy Spirit to be either the Father or the Son. Rather, we believe that the unbegotten Father, the Son begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father are of one substance or essence, because the unbegotten Father, the begotten Son and the proceeding Holy Spirit have one Godhead, but three persons, each with what is proper to it.

A heresy arose against this catholic and apostolic faith and introduced a novelty, asserting that the Son was not begotten of the Father's substance, but came into being from things that did not exist, that is, from nothing. To refute and utterly abolish this profession of impiety that had sprung up against the faith, the Greek word homoousion was laid down. It means “of one substance or essence,” and signifies that the Son was born not from things that did not exist, nor from some other substance, but from the Father. So whoever thinks homoousion should be done away with wants to claim that the Son came from nothing. But if he is not from nothing, then without doubt he is from the Father, and the Son is rightly homoousios, that is, of one substance with the Father.

(III, 2) That he is from the Father, that is, of one substance with the Father, is proved by these testimonies. The apostle says: Who, being the radiance of his glory and the very image of his substance, also upholds all things by the word of his power. And again God the Father himself, rebuking the faithlessness of unbelievers who refused to hear the voice of the Son, who abides in his substance and preached through the prophets, said: They have not heard the voice of substance. With a terrible protest he rebukes this scorning of the voice of substance, speaking to the same prophet: Take up a lament upon the mountains and mourning upon the paths of the desert, for they have failed, because there are no men; they have not heard the voice of substance, from the birds of the sky to the cattle. And again he rebukes those who turned away from the profession of one substance and would not stand in that same substance of faith, saying: If they had stood in my substance, I would surely have turned them from their evil way and from their wicked thoughts. And again it is declared most plainly that the Son is not to be confessed as outside the Father's substance, but is to be faithfully contemplated in it with the eyes of the mind, when the prophet says: Who has stood in the substance of the Lord and seen his Word?

So it was foretold long ago in the prophetic oracles that the Son is the substance of the Father, as Solomon says: For you showed your substance and your sweetness, which you have toward your children. It is clear that this flowed down from heaven to the people of Israel in the figure and image of the heavenly bread. The Lord himself explained this in the gospel when he said: It was not Moses who gave you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you bread from heaven. He was certainly indicating that he himself is that bread when he said: I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Of this the prophet David also says: Man ate the bread of angels.

(III, 3) To show still more clearly the unity of substance and the equality of Godhead of the Father and the Son, he himself says in the gospel: I am in the Father and the Father is in me, and: I and the Father are one. This refers not only to a unity of will but to one and the same substance, because he did not say, “I and the Father will one thing,” but, “We are one.” The claim of unity with the Father is declared from what they are, not only from what they will. Likewise John the evangelist says: For this reason the Jews sought to kill him, because he not only broke the sabbath but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God. This is certainly not to be attributed wholly to the Jews, because the evangelist was speaking truly of the Son when he said that he made himself equal to God.

Likewise it is written in the gospel: Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise. And: As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. Again: That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father; for equal honor is given only to equals. Again, in the same place the Son says to the Father: All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine. Again: Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father too; how can you say, Show us the Father? He would not have said this unless he were equal to the Father in all things. Again the Lord himself says: Believe in God, and believe in me. And further, to show the unity of their equality, he says:

No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. And just as the Son reveals the Father to whom he will, so the Father reveals the Son, as he himself said to Peter when Peter confessed him as the Christ, the Son of the living God: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And again the Son says: No one comes to the Father except through me, and: No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. From this it is clear that the Father and the Son, being equal, lead believers to one another. Again he says: If you had known me, you would surely have known my Father as well; from now on you know him and have seen him.

(III, 4) But since we profess that there are two natures in the Son, that is, that he is true God and true man, having a body and a soul, we hold that whatever the Scriptures relate of him with the power of surpassing majesty must be attributed to his wondrous divinity; and whatever is said of him more humbly, beneath the honor of heavenly power, we ascribe not to God the Word but to the manhood he assumed. So what we cited above belongs to his divinity, where he says: I and the Father are one, and: Whoever has seen me has seen the Father, and: Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise, and the other passages

set out above. But the things said of him according to his manhood are these: The Father is greater than I; and: I came not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me; and: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; or when he says from the cross: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? And again the prophet says in the person of the Son: From my mother's womb you are my God; or when he is shown to be lower than the angels; and a great many similar passages, which we have left out for the sake of brevity.

So the Son of God, bound by no constraint of necessity but by the free power of his divinity, took up what is ours with wonderful love, in such a way that he did not in the least give up what is his own, that is, what is divine; for the Godhead neither admits of increase nor suffers loss.
