Therefore we give thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ, who for us and for our salvation came down from heaven, redeemed us by his passion, gave us life by his death, and glorified us by his ascension; who, seated at the right hand of the Father, will come to judge the living and the dead, to bestow on the righteous the reward of eternal life and to render to the wicked and unbelieving the punishments they deserve.

(III, 5) We profess, therefore, that the Father begot the Son from himself, that is, from that which he himself is, eternally and ineffably: that he did not beget him from outside, not from nothing, not from some other matter, but that the Son was born from God. And he who was born from God is nothing other than what the Father is, and he is therefore of one substance, because a true birth does not admit a difference of kind. For if he is of a substance other than the Father's, either he is not a true Son or, what it is wicked to say, he was born degenerate. But he is a true Son, as John says:

“that we may be in his true Son.” Nor is he degenerate, since he was born true God from true God, as the same evangelist John goes on to say: “This is the true God and eternal life”; and the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth and the life.” So if he does not have his substance from elsewhere, he has it from the Father; if he has it from the Father, he is of one substance with the Father. But if he is not of one substance, then he is not from the Father but from elsewhere; for whatever a thing comes from, from that it must have its substance. All things are from nothing, but the Son is from the Father. Let anyone choose whichever of the two he wishes: either let him grant the Son a substance from the Father, or let him admit that the Son came into being from nothing.

(III, 6) But perhaps the prophetic testimony is raised against us: “Who shall declare his generation?” Yet I have not said, “Declare to me the manner or nature of the divine generation, and express in human words the mystery of so great a secret”; I have asked where he was born from. For the divine generation is indescribable, not unknowable. Indeed, it is so far from unknowable, that is, it is so far from unknown where he comes from, that the Father very often declares that he begot him from himself, and the Son that he was born from the Father. No Christian at all doubts this, as is shown in the Gospel, where the Son himself says: “But whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.” Likewise the evangelist John says: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.” So we sum up our confession in a brief statement.

If he was truly born from the Father, he is of one substance and is a true Son; but if he is not of one substance, neither is he true God. Or if he is true God and yet not of the Father's substance, then he too is unbegotten. But since he is not unbegotten, he must be a thing made, so that he would be thought to subsist from some other source, if he is not of the Father's substance. But far be it from us to believe this. For we profess that the Son is of one substance with the Father, while we detest the Sabellian heresy, which so confuses the Trinity as to say that the Father is the same as the Son, and to believe that the Holy Spirit is the same as well, not preserving three persons in unity.

(III, 7) But perhaps the objection is raised that, since the Father is unbegotten and the Son begotten, the substance of the begotten and of the unbegotten cannot be one and the same. Yet surely, if the Son were unbegotten as the Father is unbegotten, then the substance might rather be different, since each, subsisting from himself, would have no common substance with the other. But since the unbegotten Father begot the Son from himself, that is, from that which he himself is (if what that is can be said, or rather, since as it is, it cannot be said at all), it is evident that the substance of the one who begets and of the one begotten is one, for we truly profess that the Son is God from God, light from light.

For the apostle John bears witness that the Father is light, saying: “For God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all.” Likewise he says of the Son: “And the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” And further on: “That was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world.” From this it is evident that the Father and the Son are of one substance, since light and light cannot differ in substance, namely the light that begets from itself and the light that comes forth from the one who begets. Finally, so that no one might introduce between Father and Son a difference of natural light, the apostle says of the same Son: “who, being the radiance of his glory and the express image of his substance.” In this it is taught still more plainly that he is coeternal with the Father, inseparable from the Father, and of one substance with him, since radiance is always coeternal with light, since radiance is never separated from the light, and since radiance can never differ from light in the nature of its substance. For he who is the radiance of the light is also the power of God the Father; he is therefore everlasting because of the eternity of that power, and inseparable because of the unity of that brightness.

And this is what we faithfully profess: that the Son was born of the Father's substance, as God the Father himself bears the clearest witness. To show that he had begotten his own Son from the substance of his ineffable nature, and to instruct the ignorance of our frailty and raise us from visible things to invisible, he drew on the language of earthly birth as an illustration of the divine generation, saying: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” What could the Godhead have deigned to say more clearly, more plainly? By what signs, by what examples drawn from existing things, could it have conveyed the true nature of this generation better than by showing it through the word “womb”? Not that he is composed of bodily members or marked out by any outlines of limbs; but because we could not otherwise grasp the truth of the divine generation with the hearing of the mind unless we were prompted by the word for a human womb. So it can no longer be doubted that he who is known to have come forth from the Father's womb was born of God's substance.

(III, 8) Believing, then, that God the Father begot the Son from his own substance without suffering, we do not say that this substance was either divided in the Son or diminished in the Father, and so could have been subject to the defect of suffering. Far be it from us to suppose or think such things of God, for we faithfully profess that the perfect Father begot a perfect Son without diminution of himself, without any drawing off, without any weakness of suffering whatever. For whoever objects against God that, if he begot from himself, he suffered the defect of division, might as well say that he felt toil when he created all things, and that for this reason he rested on the seventh day from all his work. But neither in begetting from himself did he experience any suffering or diminution, nor in creating all things did he endure any weariness.

Indeed, so that the impassibility of the divine generation might be conveyed to us more plainly, we have been taught to profess that the Son is God from God, light from light. Consider how visible, worldly light works: when light is taken from light and arises by a kind of birth, the source itself, which gave another light from itself, is plainly neither diminished nor suffers any loss at all from the light it supplied. If something of this kind is found there, how much more rightly and fittingly must we believe of the nature of the divine and ineffable light that, begetting light from itself, it could not be diminished at all! Hence the Son is equal to the Father, not born in time but coeternal with the one who begets him, just as the radiance produced by fire is shown to be as old as the fire that produces it. Let this suffice to have said about the equality of the Father and the Son and the unity of their substance, as far as the need for brevity allows.

(III, 9) It remains for us to speak of the Holy Spirit, whom we believe to be consubstantial, coequal and coeternal with the Father and the Son, and to prove this by testimonies. For although this venerable Trinity is distinct in persons and names, it is not on that account to be believed to differ from itself or from its own eternity. Rather, the Godhead, abiding before the ages, is truly and properly believed to be in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; it cannot be divided by our interpretations, nor, on the other hand, can the Trinity itself be confused by being turned into one person.

This is the full faith; this is our belief. Therefore we do not allow gods to be either thought of or named, but we confess one God in the persons and names mentioned above. For the ineffable Godhead did not present itself within names and persons so that it could be confined or grasped by words. Rather, so that what it was might be known, it gave believers an understanding of itself in part, as much as the narrow capacity of the human mind was able to receive, as the prophet says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand.” So the deity of the Trinity is one, and in the use of this word one substance is signified, not one person. To prove this to the faithful, the Godhead itself has always come forward as a witness to itself through many and frequent attestations. Let us be permitted, then, for brevity's sake, to bring forward a few out of many; for the proof of the true majesty, though it possesses a multitude of testimonies, has no need of a multitude, since a few suffice for one who believes.

(III, 10) First, then, from the books of the Old Testament, and afterwards also from the New, we shall show that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are of one substance. The book of Genesis begins thus: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” He is the Beginning who, when the Jews asked him who he was, said: “The Beginning, who also speak to you.” And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters as Creator, holding the creation together by the power of his might. He was about to bring forth all living things from the waters, and so he himself supplied the raw elements with the warmth of his own fire; and even then, as the mystery of baptism flashed forth, the nature of water received the power of sanctification and brought forth the first living bodies into life. Accordingly David, inspired by God, testifies: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth.”

See how full this brevity is, and how clearly it returns to the mystery of unity: indicating the Father by “Lord” and the Son by the term “Word,” he named the Holy Spirit as coming from the mouth of the Most High. And so that “Word” should not be taken as a mere utterance of the voice, he asserts that the heavens were established through him; and so that the Spirit should not be thought a mere breath, he showed in him the fullness of heavenly power. For where there is power, there must be a subsisting person. And where “all” power is spoken of, it is shown not as taken away from the Father and the Son but as brought to completion in the Holy Spirit: not that he alone has what is in the Father and the Son, but that he has the whole together with both.

(III, 11) And again, when the Lord was speaking of the calling of the Gentiles, he proclaimed the Holy Spirit within the one name of the Godhead, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” And again the apostle, praying for heavenly blessings on the Corinthians, added this: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.” And so that we may confess the unity of substance in this Trinity more openly, we must also consider how God, when he was arranging the creation of the world and of man, revealed the mystery of the Trinity, saying: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” When he says “our,” he surely shows that he is not one alone; but when he speaks of image and likeness, he suggests the equality of the distinct persons. So in this same work there is an open knowledge of the Trinity, in which the plurality is not empty nor the likeness discordant, while what follows says: “And God said,” and “made,” and “God blessed.” And it must be that the author of all creation is one God.

This principle of faith is laid open and confirmed by the ancient blessing given through Moses, in which he is commanded to bless the people with the mystery of a threefold invocation. For God says to Moses: “Thus you shall bless my people, and I will bless them: The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine upon you and have mercy on you; the Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace.” The prophet David affirms this very thing, saying: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us, and let all the ends of the earth fear him.” This unity of the Trinity the heavenly powers of the angels venerate in a hymn, and singing three times with unceasing voice, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts,” they exalt his glory to the height of a single lordship.

To impress this still more plainly on the minds of the faithful, we bring forward Paul, who shared in the knowledge of the heavenly mysteries. For he says: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but the same one who gives, who works all things in all.” And he certainly taught that it is the Holy Spirit who works these various distributions according to the capacity and merit of those who share in them. For when he was setting out the different kinds of these graces, he added at the end: “But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills.”

So no room is left for doubt that the Holy Spirit is both God and the author of his own will, since he is shown most plainly to work all things and to bestow the gifts of the divine dispensation by the free choice of his own will. For where a voluntary distribution of graces is proclaimed, no condition of servitude can be seen: servitude is to be understood in the creature, but lordship and freedom in the Trinity. And to show more clearly than daylight that the Holy Spirit is of one Godhead with the Father and the Son, it is proved by the testimony of the evangelist John. For he says: “There are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one.” Does he say, “three separated by a difference of quality, or divided by some degrees of diversity across a long distance of separation”? No, he says, the three are one.

(III, 12) Now, so that the Holy Spirit may be shown ever more clearly to be one Godhead with the Father and the Son in the creation of all things, you have the Holy Spirit as Creator in the book of Job: “It is the divine Spirit,” he says, “who made me, and the Spirit of the Almighty who teaches me.” And David says: “Send forth your Spirit and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.” If renewal and re-creation are to come through the Spirit, then without doubt the first creation was not without the Spirit either. After creation, then, let us show that the Holy Spirit also gives life, as do the Father and the Son. Concerning the person of the Father the apostle says: “I charge you in the sight of God, who gives life to all things.” Christ gives life: “My sheep,” he says, “hear my voice, and I give them eternal life.” And we are given life by the Holy Spirit, as the Lord himself says: “It is the Spirit who gives life.” See, a single giving of life by the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit has been plainly shown.

(III, 13) That foreknowledge of all things and knowledge of hidden things are in the Lord, though no Christian is unaware of it, must nevertheless be shown from the book of Daniel: “O God,” he says, “who know hidden things, who foreknow all things before they come into being.” This same foreknowledge is in Christ, as the evangelist reports: “For Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him and who did not believe in him.” That he knows hidden things is clear from this: when he was exposing the secret plans of the Jews, he said, “Why do you think evil in your hearts?”

Likewise he himself made it clear that the Holy Spirit foreknows all things, when he said to the apostles: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all things and will announce to you things to come.” He who is said to announce things to come undoubtedly foreknows all things, for he searches the depths of God and knows all that is in God, as Paul records, saying: “For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.” Likewise in the same passage: “Just as no man knows the things of a man except the spirit that is in him, so no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.”

(III, 14) To understand the power of the Holy Spirit, let us bring forward a few of the fearful examples. A deceitful disciple, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles, had sold a property; keeping back part of the money, he laid the rest at the apostles' feet as though it were the whole. He offended the Holy Spirit, from whom he thought he could hide. But what did blessed Peter say to him at once? “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, so that you lied to the Holy Spirit?” And further on: “You have not lied to men but to God.” And so, struck down by the power of the one to whom he had wanted to lie, he breathed his last. What blessed Peter wants us to understand the Holy Spirit to be here is surely clear, since he says: “You have not lied to men but to God.” It is evident, then, that whoever lies to the Holy Spirit lies to God, and whoever believes in the Holy Spirit believes in God.

The Lord shows something similar, indeed something stronger, in the Gospel: “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.” See, by a fearful sentence he declares that the sin of one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit cannot be forgiven. Compare with this sentence what is written in the book of Kings: “If a man sins against a man, they will pray for him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” If, then, blaspheming against the Holy Spirit and sinning against God are alike, that is, an inexpiable crime, everyone now recognizes how great the Holy Spirit is.

(III, 15) That God is present everywhere and fills all things we learn from the mouth of Isaiah: “I am a God near at hand,” he says, “and not far off. If a man hides himself in secret places, shall I then not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” And what does the Saviour say in the Gospel about his own presence everywhere? “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name,” he says, “there am I in the midst of them.” Likewise, that the Holy Spirit is present everywhere, the prophet says in the person of God: “I am among you, and my Spirit stands in your midst.” And Solomon says: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which holds all things together has knowledge of every voice.” Likewise David says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present; if I take my wings straight on and dwell in the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me and your right hand will hold me.”

(III, 16) God dwells in his saints according to the promise in which he had said: “I will dwell in them.” And what the Lord Jesus says in the Gospel, “Abide in me, and I in you,” Paul confirms, saying: “Do you not know that Jesus Christ is in you?” All this is fulfilled by the indwelling of the Spirit, as John records: “By this,” he says, “we know that he is in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.” Likewise Paul too: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” And again he says: “Glorify and carry God in your body.” Which God? Surely the Holy Spirit, whose temple we are seen to be.

(III, 17) That the Father reproves, the Son reproves, and the Holy Spirit reproves is to be proved thus. In the forty-ninth psalm we read: “But to the sinner God says”; and further on: “I will reprove you and set it before your face.” Likewise David, in prayer, says to Christ: “Lord, do not reprove me in your anger,” for he himself is to come to reprove all flesh. And what does the Saviour say of the Holy Spirit in the Gospel? “When the Paraclete comes,” he says, “he will reprove the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgment.” Foreseeing this, David cried out to the Lord: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?”

(III, 18) That the Father is good, the Son is good and the Holy Spirit is good is proved thus. The prophet says: “You are good, O Lord, and in your goodness teach me your statutes.” And the Only-begotten says of himself: “I am the good shepherd.” Likewise, of the Holy Spirit David says in a psalm: “Your good Spirit will lead me into the right land.”

(III, 19) And who could pass over in silence that dignity of the Holy Spirit? The ancient prophets used to cry out, "Thus says the Lord." Christ, when he came, took this saying back into his own person, saying, "But I say to you." And what did the new prophets cry out? As the prophet Agabus says in the Acts of the Apostles, "Thus says the Holy Spirit"; and Paul writes to Timothy, "The Spirit expressly says." This way of speaking shows plainly that there is no difference within the Trinity. Paul says that he was called and sent by God the Father and by Christ: "Paul," he says, "an apostle, not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father." But in the Acts of the Apostles he says that he was set apart and sent by the Holy Spirit, for it is written there: "Thus says the Holy Spirit: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them." And a little later: "So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia." Again in the same book: "Keep watch over yourselves and over the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops."

(III, 20) Let no one think the Holy Spirit something to be looked down on because he is called the Paraclete. For "Paraclete" means advocate, or rather comforter, in the Latin tongue, and this title is shared by the Son of God as well, as John says: "I write these things to you so that you may not sin; but if anyone does sin, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ." And the Lord himself, when he says to the apostles, "The Father will send you another Paraclete," without doubt shows that he too is a Paraclete, since he says "another Paraclete." Nor is this name of Paraclete foreign to the Father, for it is a name of kindness, not of nature.

So Paul writes to the Corinthians: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us." And although the Father is called Comforter, the Son is called Comforter, and the Holy Spirit too is called Comforter, yet one comfort is given to us by the Trinity, just as there is one forgiveness of sins, as the Apostle affirms: "You were washed," he says, "and justified, and you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God." We could bring forward still more testimonies from the divine Scriptures which, in keeping with the sacrament of baptism, show the Trinity to be of one glory, one working and one power. But since these are enough to give the wise full understanding, we have passed over many things for the sake of brevity.
(III, 21) Let us then sum up what we have said.

If the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; if he sets free; if he is Lord and sanctifies; if he creates with the Father and the Son, and if he gives life; if he has foreknowledge with the Father and the Son; if he is everywhere and fills all things; if he dwells in the elect; if he convicts the world; if he judges; if he is good and upright; if it is proclaimed of him, “Thus says the Holy Spirit”; if he appoints prophets; if he sends apostles; if he sets bishops over the churches; if he is the Comforter; if he distributes all things as he wills; if he washes and justifies; if he slays those who put him to the test; if whoever blasphemes him has no forgiveness either in this age or in the age to come, which is surely proper to God alone: since all this is so, why is there doubt that he is God, when by the greatness of his works he himself shows what he is? Surely he who is no stranger to the work of mighty deeds is no stranger to the majesty of the Father and the Son.

It is in vain that the name of Godhead is denied to him whose power cannot be denied; in vain am I forbidden to worship with the Father and the Son him whom I am required to confess with the Father and the Son. If he, with the Father and the Son, bestows on me forgiveness of sins, bestows sanctification and eternal life, I am utterly ungrateful and impious if I do not give glory to him with the Father and the Son. Or if he is not to be worshipped with the Father and the Son, then neither is he to be confessed in baptism. But if he must by all means be confessed, according to the Lord’s word and the tradition of the apostles, so that our faith may not be only half complete, who can forbid me to worship him? For in him in whom I am commanded to believe, to him also I shall rightly offer my prayers. I will therefore worship the Father, I will worship the Son, and I will worship the Holy Spirit, with one and the same adoration.

If anyone thinks this hard, let him hear how David urges the faithful to the worship of God: “Worship,” he says, “his footstool.” If it is an act of religion to worship his footstool, how much more religious it is to worship his Spirit! That Spirit, surely, whom blessed Peter proclaimed in such lofty terms, saying: “by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, into whom the angels long to look.” If the angels long to look upon him, how much more ought we, mortal men, not to look down on him, lest it be said to us too, as it was said to the Jews: “You always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did.”

(III, 21) But if these things, so many and so great, do not move the soul to worship the Holy Spirit, hear now something stronger still. For this is how Paul instructs the prophets of the Church, in whom and through whom the Holy Spirit was certainly speaking: “If all prophesy,” he says, “and an unbeliever or an outsider comes in, he is convicted by all, he is examined by all, and the secrets of his heart are laid bare; and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.” And surely the Holy Spirit is in those who prophesy. If, then, unbelievers fall on their faces and worship the Holy Spirit when terrified [?], and confess him against their will, how much more fitting is it for the faithful to worship the Holy Spirit willingly and from the heart! Yet the Holy Spirit is not worshipped separately, after the manner of the pagans, just as the Son is not worshipped separately because he is at the right hand of the Father. Rather, when we worship the Father, we believe that we also worship the Son and the Holy Spirit; for when we call upon the Son we believe that we are calling upon the Father, and when we pray to the Father we trust that we are heard by the Son, as the Lord himself said: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do it, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.” And if the Holy Spirit is worshipped, he whose Spirit he is is surely worshipped too.

No one is unaware of this: nothing can be added to or taken from the divine majesty by human prayers. Rather, each person, according to the purpose of his own will, either gains glory for himself by faithful worship or everlasting shame by stubborn resistance. For it is certain that contention and pride bring condemnation, while reverence looks for the fruit of devotion. Why, then, should the faithful not honor the Trinity in its fullness, to which they trust they belong, in whose name they have been reborn, and whose servants they glory to be called? For just as men are called men of God after the name of God the Father, as Elijah was called a man of God and Moses was called a man of God, so we are called Christians after Christ, and so too we are called spiritual after the Spirit. If, then, someone is called a man of God and is not a Christian, he is nothing; and if he is called a Christian and is not spiritual, let him not be too confident of his salvation.

(III, 23) Let us therefore hold, in accordance with the confession of saving baptism, a complete faith in the Trinity and a single devotion of piety. Let us not imagine, after the manner of the pagans, a diversity of powers, nor suspect that there is any creature in the Trinity as regards Godhead. Nor let us be moved by the stumbling block of the Jews, who deny the Son of God and do not worship the Spirit. Rather, worshipping and magnifying the perfect Trinity, let us hold in our conscience what we say with our lips in the sacred mysteries: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.” In saying “holy” three times we confess one omnipotence, for there is one worship and one glorification of the Trinity; so that we may hear the apostle as the Corinthians heard him: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.”

This is our faith, founded on the traditions of the Gospels and the apostles and on the fellowship of all the catholic churches that are in this world. In it, by the grace of almighty God, we trust and hope to remain until the end of this life.

Delivered on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, by Januarius of Zattara and Villaticus of Casae Medianae, bishops of Numidia, and Boniface of Foratiana and Boniface of Gatiana, bishops of Byzacena.
BOOK THREE.

(IV, 1) When our booklet was presented and read out, they could not bear the light of truth with their blind eyes. They raged, gnashing their teeth and shouting, and took it badly that we had called ourselves Catholics. At once they went to the king with lies about us, saying that we had raised an uproar to escape the hearing. Inflamed at that very hour and believing the lie, he hurried to do what he wanted.

He already had a decree drawn up, and he secretly sent his men with it through the various provinces. So while the bishops were held in Carthage, he closed the churches of all Africa on a single day and gave all the property of the bishops and the churches as a gift to his own bishops. Not knowing what they were saying or what they were asserting, they were not ashamed to turn against us the law that our Christian emperors had long ago issued against them and other heretics for the honour of the Catholic Church, and they added much of their own, as the tyrant's power saw fit. This is the text of the law as it was issued and posted:

(IV, 2) "Huneric, King of the Vandals and Alans, to all the peoples subject to our kingdom. It is a proof of triumphal and royal majesty to turn evil counsels back on those who devised them, for whoever contrives some wickedness has only himself to blame for what befalls him. In this matter our clemency has followed the will of divine judgment. Just as it has the deeds of each person weighed, whether good or perhaps the opposite, so it also has each repaid as his deeds deserved. Therefore, provoked by those who believed that the command of our father of glorious memory, or of our own mildness, could be despised, we take up the censure of severity.

For we made it known to all peoples by official edicts that the homoousian priests should hold no assemblies in the allotments of the Vandals, nor claim for themselves any of their mysteries, which pollute rather than sanctify. When we saw that this had been neglected, and that very many were found who said they kept the whole rule of faith, it is well known that all of them were afterwards warned. They were granted in advance a period of nine months for the debate [?], so that whatever they proposed might be made ready, and they were to assemble without any fear on the first of February in the eighth year of our reign.

While they were flocking here to the city of Carthage, it is known that after the appointed time had passed we granted them a further postponement of some days. When they declared that they were ready for the debate, on the first day our venerable bishops proposed to them that they should prove the homoousion properly from the divine Scriptures, as they had been warned to do, or else condemn outright what had been cut away by more than a thousand bishops from the whole world at the Council of Ariminum and at Seleucia.

This they utterly refused to do, and instead turned everything toward sedition by a populace they had stirred up. Indeed, on the second day too, when we ordered them to answer about that same faith as had been proposed, they evidently adopted such recklessness that they threw everything into confusion with sedition and shouting and made sure the debate never took place at all.

Since they provoked this, we decreed that their churches should be closed. We set this condition: they would stay closed until they were willing to come to the proposed debate. This they refused to do, with an obstinacy they evidently took from wicked counsels. It is therefore necessary and entirely just to turn back on them the contents of those very laws which emperors of various times, whom they had led into error with them, once happened to promulgate.

The tenor of those laws is plainly this. No church was to be open except to the bishops of their superstition. Nowhere were others to be allowed to hold gatherings or assemblies, or to possess or build churches at all, whether in cities or in even the smallest places; whatever they had taken was to be joined to the resources of the treasury. Moreover, their estates were to pass to the bishops and be joined to the churches of their faith. Such people were not to be allowed to stay in any place whatever, but were to be made exiles from all cities and places. They were to have no power at all to baptize, or perhaps to dispute about religion, and no licence to ordain bishops, priests or any others who belong to the clergy. A severe penalty was laid down: both those who let themselves receive such honours and the ordainers themselves were to be fined ten pounds of gold each. It was added that they should have no opportunity or access to petition, and that even if they had obtained any special privileges, these would not help them. And if they persisted in this ruinous course, they were to be deprived of their property and sent into exile under suitable escort.

The aforesaid emperors raged in the same way against the laity too. They were wholly forbidden to give, to make a will, or to receive anything left them by others, whether by trust, by legacy, by gift, by a bequest made in view of death, by any codicil, or perhaps by other writings. Even those who served in their palaces were made subject to the heaviest condemnation according to their rank, so that they would be stripped of every privilege of honour and incur infamy, and such persons would know they were liable to public criminal charges. For the officials of the various judges, too, a penalty of thirty pounds of silver was set. If it had to be imposed five times on those persisting in error, then at last such people were to be convicted, subdued with beatings and sent into exile.

Next, they had ordered all the books of the priests whom they were persecuting to be thrown into the fire. We command the same to be done to books of this kind, by which wickedness has persuaded itself of the error of that name. For, as has been said, they had ordered the following to be observed for each class of person: illustres were to pay fifty pounds of gold each, spectabiles forty pounds of gold, senators thirty pounds of gold, principales twenty pounds of gold, sacerdotales thirty pounds of gold, decurions five pounds of gold, merchants five pounds of gold, plebeians five pounds of gold, and circumcellions ten pounds of silver. And if any persisted in this ruinous course, all their property was to be confiscated and they were to be punished with exile.

They are also seen to have laid such a penalty on city councils, as well as on the stewards and lessees of estates, that if these chose to hide such people, did not report them, and did not present them in court once they were held, they themselves would be liable to the penalty. For lessees of the royal estates this fine was set: whatever they paid to the royal house, they would be forced to pay the same amount again to the treasury as a penalty. We have decreed that this be observed generally for all lessees and landholders who decide to persist in that same superstition. For judges, too, who did not press this matter with the utmost urgency, the penalty of proscription and capital punishment was laid down. Of the heads of their staffs, three were to be punished, and the rest were to be fined twenty pounds of gold.

"It is therefore necessary that the homoousians be bound by these constitutions: all who are known to have held, and still to hold, the substance of such an evil persuasion. We decree that they are to abstain from all the things listed above, and that they will be prosecuted through the councils of all the cities; and the same applies to judges who are shown to have been negligent in this and to have inflicted [?] dire punishments on various people. All who are entangled in the errors of the aforesaid homoousian faith, which was condemned beforehand by an entire council of so great a number of bishops, we command to abstain from all the aforesaid dealings and contracts. Let them know that nothing is permitted to them, and that the same penalty awaits and binds them all if they have not converted, by the day of the Kalends of June in the eighth year of our reign, to the true religion which we revere and worship. Our piety has set this appointed day so that pardon may not be denied to those who condemn their error, and so that fitting punishments may restrain obstinate minds.

Those who remain in that same error, whether they are employed in the service of our household or perhaps placed in charge of various offices and duties, shall be compelled to pay the fines listed above according to their rank. Nothing that any such person may perhaps have obtained by stealth will help him. Our proclamation also orders that, for private persons of whatever rank and station, what the aforesaid laws were seen to lay down about such people be observed, so that they are subjected to fitting penalties. Provincial judges who neglect to carry out what has been decreed shall, we decree, be bound by the penalty laid down above for such people.

By this decree we ordain that all the churches, those of the whole clergy of the aforesaid name, situated in whatever lands and regions are held, by divine favour, under the rule of our dominion, together with the property belonging to them, shall pass to the true worshippers of the divine majesty, that is, to our priests. We do not doubt that what has been justly conferred on the holy bishops does more to feed the poor. We therefore command that this law, flowing from the fountain of justice, be made known to all, so that no one may claim he did not know what was ordered. We wish you good health. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, at Carthage."

(IV, 3) After these deadly edicts, steeped in poison, he ordered all the bishops who had gathered at Carthage, whose churches, houses and property had already been seized, to be stripped in the lodgings where they were staying and then driven outside the wall. They were left no animal, no servant, not even the change of clothes they had with them. He further ordered that no one should take any of them in or give them food, and that whoever tried to do so out of compassion would be burned along with his whole house.

The bishops who had been thrown out acted wisely then: though they had to beg, they did not go away from there. If they had left, they would simply have been brought back by force, and the Arians would have claimed falsely, as indeed they did, that they had fled the debate. Besides, they had nowhere left to return to, since their churches, property and houses had been seized. So while they lay groaning around the walls under the open sky, it happened that the impious king went out to the baths. All of them chose to go and meet him, saying: "Why are we afflicted like this? What evils have we committed to suffer these things? If we were assembled for a debate, why have we been stripped? Why are we disgraced, why are we put off? Why are we left without our churches and homes, outside the city, suffering hunger and nakedness and wallowing in filth?" He glared at them and, before he had even heard their petition, ordered horses with their riders to be driven at them, so that by such violence they might not only be trampled but even killed. Many of them were trampled then, especially the old and the infirm.

(IV, 4) After that, these men of God were ordered to assemble at a place called the Temple of Memory, not knowing that a trap had been laid for them. When they arrived, they were shown a rolled-up document and told, with the cunning of the serpent: "Our lord King Huneric grieves that you have shown contempt and still delay to obey his will that you adopt the religion he holds. Nevertheless, he has now formed a kind intention toward you: if you swear to do what this document contains, he will let you return to your churches and your homes." To this all the bishops replied: "We always say, have said, and will say: we are Christians, we are bishops, we hold the one true apostolic faith."

After this confession of faith there was a short silence, and then the king's envoys hurried to extract an oath from the bishops. At that the blessed bishops Hortulanus and Florentianus, speaking for all and together with all, said: "Are we irrational animals, to swear lightly or rashly without knowing what the document contains?" So the king's envoys hastened to reveal to them the contents of the writing, which was dressed up in words of this kind.

The slanderous text ran as follows: "Swear that after the death of our lord the king you want his son Hilderic to be king, and that none of you will send letters to lands overseas. If you give your oath on this, he will restore you to your churches." Then many, in their pious simplicity, thought of taking the oath even against the divine prohibition, so that the people of God would not say afterward that their churches had not been restored through the fault of the priests who refused to swear. Other bishops, more shrewd, saw through the deceitful trick and refused to swear at all, saying that it was forbidden by the authority of the Gospel, since the Lord himself says: "You shall not swear at all." The king's officials said to them: "Let those who mean to swear stand to one side." When they had done so, notaries wrote down what each one said and what city he came from, and the same was done for those who did not swear. At once both groups were placed under guard.

(IV, 5) Afterwards the hidden fraud came to light. Those who had sworn were told: "Because you were willing to swear against the command of the Gospel, the king has ordered that you shall never see your cities and churches again. Instead you are banished and will receive fields to farm as coloni, on condition that you do not sing psalms or pray, do not carry a book in your hands to read, do not baptize or ordain, and do not presume to reconcile anyone." Likewise he said to those who had not sworn: "You refused to swear because you do not want our lord's son to reign. For this reason you are ordered to be banished to the island of Corsica, to cut timber for the royal ships."

(V, 1) Then that beast, thirsting for the blood of the innocent, went further. While the bishops had not yet been sent into exile, he dispatched the cruellest torturers all at once through every province of the land of Africa, so that no house or place was left without wailing and mourning. No age and no sex was spared, except those who yielded to their will. Some they beat with clubs, some they hanged, others they burned with fire. Women, and especially noblewomen, they tortured stark naked in full public view, against the laws of nature.

Of these I will name, quickly and briefly, our own Dionysia. When they saw that she was not only bold but also more beautiful than the other matrons, they first tried to strip her and make her ready for the rods. Confident in her Lord, she begged them, saying: "Torture me however you like, but do not expose my modest body." They raged all the more, stripped her of her clothes and set her on a raised spot, making her a spectacle for everyone. Under the blows of the rods, while streams of blood were flowing over her whole body, she said boldly: "Servants of the devil, what you think you are doing to disgrace me is my very glory." And because she was full of knowledge of the divine Scriptures, though hard pressed by torments and already a martyr herself, she strengthened others for martyrdom, and by her holy example she freed almost her whole home town.

She saw that her only son, still very young and delicate, was terrified by fear of the torments. She rebuked him with her eyes and reproved him with a mother's authority, and so strengthened him that he became much braver than his mother. As he was put under the cruel lash, she said to him: "Remember, my son, that we were baptized in the name of the Trinity in our mother the Catholic Church. Let us not lose the garment of our salvation, so that the one who invited us does not come, find us without a wedding garment, and say to his servants: Throw him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth. The punishment to fear is the one that never ends; the life to desire is the one possessed forever." Strengthening her son with such words, she quickly made him a martyr.

This venerable youth, Majoricus by name, gave up his spirit in the contest of confession and finished the course that wins the palm. Embracing her sacrifice and thanking the Lord as loudly as she could, she chose, in the joy of the hope to come, to bury him in her own house, so that whenever she pours out prayers to the Trinity over his tomb she may be confident that she is never separated from her son. How many were won for God through her in that city, as we have said, would take too long to tell. As for her sister Dativa, Leontia the daughter of the holy bishop Germanus, Dativa's kinsman the venerable physician Aemilius, the devout Tertius, famous for his confession of the Trinity, and Boniface of Sibida: how much they endured, and with what tortures they were torn apart, let anyone who can tell it in order.

(V, 2) And who could describe the punishments that Servus of the city of Thuburbo Majus, a man of good family and noble birth, endured for Christ? After beatings with countless clubs he was hoisted again and again with pulleys and left hanging over the whole city. Now they raised him high; then, with a quick release of the hemp ropes, he dropped with the full weight of his body onto the paving stones of the streets, like a stone falling on stones. Often, too, he was dragged and scraped over very sharp stones, so that you could see his skin torn loose and hanging from his sides, back and belly. In Geiseric's time he had already endured much the same so as not to betray the secrets of a friend; how much more now, to guard the sacraments of his faith! And if he kept faith loyally with a man for nothing, how much more does he owe to the One who will reward faith!

(V, 3) In the city of Culusi I cannot report all that was done, since no human being could count even the number of the martyrs and confessors. There a certain matron, Victoria, true to her name, was being burned in the sight of the crowd while she hung for a long time. Her husband, already lost, pleaded with her in front of their children: "What are you suffering for, wife? If you despise me, at least have pity on these little ones you bore, you wicked woman. Why do you forget your own womb and count as nothing the children you brought forth with groaning? Where are the bonds of married love? Where are the ties of partnership which the marriage contract, drawn up between us long ago in honourable form, established? Look at your children and your husband, I beg you, and hurry to obey the royal command, so that you may escape the torments still hanging over you and be given back to me and to our children." But she listened neither to her children's weeping nor to the serpent's blandishments; lifting her love far above the earth, she despised the world and its desires. Her shoulders were wrenched out of joint by the long hanging, and when even her torturers saw that she was dead, they took her down, lifeless in every part. Afterwards she related that a certain virgin had stood beside her and touched each of her limbs, and that she had been healed at once.

(V, 4) How I should praise Victorian, a citizen of Hadrumetum who was then proconsul of Carthage, I do not know; words fail me. No one in the regions of Africa was richer than he, and even the impious king regarded him as completely trustworthy in the affairs he regularly entrusted to him. The king sent him a friendly message, telling him he would rank him above everyone if he readily agreed to his command. But that man of God, with great confidence, gave this reply to those sent to him: "Secure in God and in Christ my Lord, I tell you to say this to the king: let him put me to the fire, throw me to the beasts, torture me with every kind of torment; if I consent, I was baptized in the Catholic Church in vain. For even if this present life were the only one, and we did not hope for another, eternal life, the one that truly is, I still would not do this: glory for a little while, for a time, and prove ungrateful to my creditor, who entrusted his faith to me." At this the tyrant was roused to fury, and no human words could describe for how long and with what punishments he afflicted him. Rejoicing in the Lord and finishing his course happily, he received the martyr's crown.

(V, 5) And who could describe the martyrs' struggles at the city of Tambaia? There two brothers from the city of Aquae Regiae, secure in the Lord, swore to each other that they would ask the torturers to subject them both to the same penalty and the same punishment. On the first day of hanging, with heavy stones tied to their feet, they hung all day long, and one of them asked to be taken down and given a respite. His brother, afraid that he would deny the faith, cried out even as he hung: "No, no, brother! That is not what we swore to Christ. I will accuse you when we come before his terrible throne, for we swore over his body and blood that we would suffer for him together." By saying this and much more he strengthened his brother for the battle of his passion, and the brother cried out in a loud voice: "Use whatever punishments you like and press the Christians with cruel torments; whatever my brother does, I will do too." How many red-hot plates burned them, what hooks tore furrows in them, what tortures racked them, the outcome itself shows: the torturers themselves drove them from their sight, saying, "The whole people is imitating these men, so that no one at all is converting to our religion." Above all, no bruises and no traces of their punishments could be seen on them at all.

(V, 6) Let me hasten now to relate, to the praise of God, what was done at Tipasa, a city of Greater Mauretania. When its people saw that an Arian bishop, formerly a notary of Cyrila, had been ordained for their city to destroy souls, the whole city fled together by ship to Spain, which lies close by. Only a very few were left behind, who had found no way to sail. The Arian bishop began to pressure them, first with flattery and then with threats, to make them Arians. But, strong in the Lord, they not only laughed at the madness of the man trying to persuade them, but even began to celebrate the divine mysteries openly, gathered together in one house. When he learned of this, he secretly sent a report against them to Carthage.

When this became known to the king, he angrily sent a certain count with orders that, in the middle of the forum and with the whole province gathered there, their tongues and right hands should be cut off at the root. When this had been done, by the gift of the Holy Spirit they spoke, and still speak, just as they had spoken before. But if anyone wants to disbelieve this, let him go now to Constantinople, and there he will find one of them, the subdeacon Reparatus, speaking polished speech without any impediment. For this reason he is held in very great honour in the palace of the emperor Zeno, and the empress in particular treats him with remarkable reverence.

(V, 7) But who could find fitting words to set out, or even to gather together, the many kinds of punishment that the Vandals inflicted on the orders of their king, even on their own people? Even about what was done at Carthage itself, a writer who tried to set it down case by case, even without ornament of style, could not so much as name the tortures. The facts themselves, still plain to see today, show it. You may observe some without hands, others without eyes, others without feet, others with their noses and ears cut off. You may see others whose heads, which once stood upright, have sunk down between their shoulder blades through excessive hanging, their shoulders wrenched out of place [?]. For the torturers would hang them continuously from high buildings, and by pushing with their hands set the ropes swinging, so that the hanging man was swung this way and that through the empty air. Sometimes the ropes broke, and they crashed down with great force from that height: very many lost their brains along with their eyes, others had their bones broken and gave up the spirit at once, and others breathed their last a little later.

But whoever thinks this a fable, let him ask Uranius, Zeno's envoy, in whose presence these things were done with particular intent, because on coming to Carthage he had boasted that he had come to defend the Catholic churches. To show him that he feared no one, the tyrant stationed more numerous and crueler torturers in the very squares and streets through which envoys customarily pass on their way up to the palace and back down. This was, of course, an insult to the empire itself and a mark of the dregs to which our failing age has now sunk.

(V, 8) At that time too a woman named Dagila, the wife of one of the king's cellarers, who had already been a confessor many times in the days of Geiseric, a noble and delicate lady, was utterly broken with whips and cudgels and banished to a dry and trackless place of exile, where no human being could find a way to come to her even to offer comfort. She left her home, her husband and her sons with joy. Later, it is said, she was offered a transfer to a less desolate desert, where she could enjoy the comfort of companions if she wished. But she, believing it a great joy to be where there was no human consolation at all, begged that this not be done.

(V, 9) Then too, when the shepherd Eugenius had already been sent into exile, the entire clergy of the church of Carthage, wasted by beatings and hunger, some five hundred or more, among whom were a great many little boys who served as lectors, were handed over, rejoicing in the Lord, to cruel exile far away. But I must not pass over in silence the freedom of speech of the deacon Muritta, bolder than the rest, at the time when they were being beaten in the middle of the city. There was a man named Elpidophorus, extremely cruel and savage, who had been given the task of tearing the limbs of Christ's confessors with raging tortures. Long before, he had been baptized among us in the church of Faustus, and the venerable deacon Muritta had received him, newly reborn, from the basin of the font. But afterward, when he apostatized, he showed such savagery against the church of God that he was found to be the foremost executor of the persecution. What more need I say?

When the priests were first summoned in order to be wasted by tortures, the aforementioned Muritta was subjected to punishment after the archdeacon Salutaris, for he was second in the order of ministers. As the venerable old man began to be stretched out, with Elpidophorus sitting there and raging, before he was stripped he happened to be carrying, secretly and unknown to anyone, the cloths with which he had long ago covered Elpidophorus when receiving him from the font. Shaking them out and spreading them for all to see, he is said to have moved the whole city to weeping and tears with these words:

"These are the linens, Elpidophorus, minister of error, which will accuse you when the majesty of the Judge comes. I will keep them carefully as a witness to your perdition, to plunge you into the abyss of the sulphurous pit. These wrapped you spotless as you rose from the font; these will pursue you all the more fiercely when you come into possession of flaming Gehenna, because you have clothed yourself with cursing as with a garment, tearing apart and casting away the sacrament of true baptism and faith. What will you do, wretch, when the servants of the householder begin to gather the invited guests to the royal supper? Then the King, at last calling you, will see you stripped of the wedding robe and will be terribly angry, and he will say to you: 'Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment? I do not see what I bestowed; I do not recognize what I gave. You have lost the soldier's cloak which I wove for ten months on the loom of a virgin's body, which I stretched on the frame of the cross, cleansed with water and adorned with the purple of my blood. I do not see the beauty of my seal; I do not see the mark of the Trinity. Such a man cannot take part in my feast.

Bind him hand and foot with his own cords, since of his own will he chose to separate himself from those who were once his Catholic brothers. He himself stretched out the ropes, knotted together into a noose, with which he both bound himself and kept others from coming to this banquet. Beside the path he set a stumbling block for many; and now I have cast him out of my banquet with lasting shame and everlasting disgrace.'" As Muritta said these and other things, Elpidophorus fell silent and was scorched by the fire of conscience before the eternal fire.

(V, 10) So all of them, offering their backs to the lash, set out eagerly for exile. While they were still on the road of their long journey, at the urging of the Arian bishops, merciless and violent men were sent after them to take away cruelly whatever Christian compassion might have given them to help them live. Then each of them perhaps sang the more gladly: "Naked I came out of my mother's womb; naked I must go into exile, for the Lord knows how to give food to the hungry and to clothe people in the desert." Two Vandals as well, who had often been confessors under Geiseric, went into exile with these clerics, accompanied by their mother and despising all their wealth.

From the multitude of confessors setting out, that is, the clergy of the church of Carthage, at the prompting of a certain lector, the lost Teucharius, the king said that twelve little boys should be separated by his designation, whom Teucharius knew to be tuneful, vigorous and skilled in the melodies of chant, and whom he himself, when he was a Catholic, had once had as pupils. At once, at his prompting, post-horses were sent in haste, and by the force of barbarian fury the twelve boys were called back from the road. They were separated from the flock of the saints in body, not in spirit. Fearing to fall headlong, with sighs and tears they clung with their hands to the knees of their companions so as not to be torn away. Yet heretical violence separated them with threatening swords and brought them back to Carthage.

But when they were worked on with coaxing [?], as is done with children of that age, they proved wiser than their years, and so as not to fall asleep in death, they lit for themselves the lamp of the gospel's light. The Arians were deeply indignant at this and ashamed to have been beaten by boys. Inflamed with anger, they ordered them to be beaten with cudgels again and again, though only a very few days before they had already torn them apart with various beatings. Wounds were laid upon wounds, and the punishment, renewed, grew still crueler. But with the Lord strengthening them, it came about that their tender age did not give way under the pain; rather, their spirit grew stronger in faith. Now Carthage honours them with wonderful affection and looks on these boys as a choir of twelve apostles. They live together, eat together, sing psalms together, and glory together in the Lord.

In those days two merchants of the same city, Frumentius and another Frumentius, were crowned with a glorious martyrdom. At that time too seven brothers, brothers not by nature but by grace, who lived together in a monastery, completed the contest of confession and attained the unfading crown [namely, Liberatus the abbot, Boniface the deacon, Rusticus the subdeacon, Rogatus a monk, Septimus a monk and Maximus a monk].

(V, 11) At that time the Arian bishops, priests and clergy raged even more cruelly, together with the king and the Vandals. They themselves, with their clergy, ran about everywhere girded with swords to carry on the persecution. Such was a certain bishop among them, crueler than the rest, named Antonius, who committed such wicked and unbelievable acts against our people that they cannot be told. He lived in a city near the desert, bordering on the province of Tripolitania. Like an insatiable beast thirsting for Catholic blood, he roamed here and there, roaring in search of prey.

The impious Huneric, knowing Antonius' ferocity, decided to banish holy Eugenius to those very parts of the desert. When Antonius received him into his custody, he confined him so strictly that he let no one go in to see him, and he planned besides to destroy him by various tortures, whether by plotting or by punishment. But holy Eugenius, as he lamented the hardships of our persecution, wore down his aged body with the roughness of haircloth, and lying on the bare ground he watered his bed of sackcloth with showers of tears, until at length he contracted the disease of paralysis.

At this news the Arian turned to joy and hurried to the cell where the man of God was in exile. When he saw that the true bishop, under the pressure of his affliction, could only bring out stammering words, he thought he would finish off once and for all the man he did not want to survive. He ordered harsh and very sour vinegar to be found, and when it had been brought, he forced it down the venerable old man's throat as he refused and resisted. For if our common Lord, who had come for the very purpose of drinking, would not drink it when he had tasted it, how much more would this servant and faithful confessor have utterly refused it, had heretical savagery not forced it on him! From this vinegar, which was especially harmful to that ailment, the disease grew worse; but the compassion of Christ mercifully came to his aid and later restored him to health.

(V, 12) Another of our bishops, Habetdeum, was likewise banished to the city of Tamallume, where Antonius was, and the facts themselves show how much Antonius was able to harass him there. He afflicted him with persecutions of every kind but could not make him an Arian, and he saw that the soldier of Christ remained ever constant in his confession. For he had made a promise to his people, saying, "If I do not make him one of our religion, let me not be Antonius!" But when he fell short of his promise, at the devil's suggestion he thought of another plan.

He bound the bishop hand and foot with heavy chains, stopped his mouth so that his tongue could not cry out, and sprinkled water over his body, which he imagined to be the water of rebaptism. As if he could bind the conscience along with the body! As if he were not present who hears the groans of those in chains and searches the secrets of the heart! As if lying water could overcome the purpose of so firm a will, which the man of God had already sent up to heaven as his envoy by means of his tears! At once he freed the man from his chains and, as if rejoicing, went on to say: "See, brother Habetdeum, now you have been made one of our Christians. What more can you do now but consent to the king's will?" Habetdeum answered him: "Wicked Antonius, the condemnation of death lies where the will's consent is obtained. I, holding fast to my faith and confessing again and again in words what I believe and have always believed, have defended it by crying out. And even after you bound me in chains and blocked up the door of my mouth, in the courtroom of my heart I drew up a record of the violence done to me, with angels as the scribes, and sent it to my Emperor to read."
(V, 13) This violence of the tyrants was, in fact, everywhere.

Vandals had been posted everywhere for this very purpose: to seize travellers on the roads and bring them to their priests to have their throats cut. When they had killed them with the sword of that deceitful water, they would hand them a written token of their damnation, so that they would not be dragged off elsewhere by the same violence. For neither private persons nor merchants were allowed to travel anywhere unless the poor wretches could show their own death written down and marked with a sign. Christ had long ago revealed this to his servant John in the Revelation, where he says: No one will be allowed to buy or sell anything except the one who has the mark of the beast on his forehead and on his hand.

Their bishops and presbyters, too, would go round the villages and towns at night with a band of armed men. Scorning the doorposts, these robbers of souls went in carrying water and the sword. Those they found at home, some perhaps asleep in their beds, they sprinkled with a fiery shower like lightning, and with demonic shouting they called them their Christians, which showed it to be a game of their heresy rather than any kind of religion. The less understanding and the faint-hearted believed that the sacrilege of pollution had been accomplished in them, but the wiser rejoiced that what had been forced on them unwilling and asleep could do them no harm. At that very hour many threw ashes on their heads; others, because the thing had been done, covered themselves in mournful sackcloth; some smeared themselves with stinking mud; and the linen garments violently put on them they tore apart thread by thread and, with the hand of faith, flung them into latrines and foul places.

(V, 14) By such violence, before our own eyes, there at Carthage, the son of a certain nobleman, about seven years old, was separated from his parents on the orders of Cyrila. His mother, casting aside a matron's modesty, ran after the abductors through the whole city with her hair unbound, while the little child cried out as best he could: "I am a Christian, I am a Christian, by Saint Stephen I am a Christian!" They stopped his mouth and plunged his innocent infancy into their pool.

It is well established that the same was done to the sons of the venerable physician Liberatus. When by the king's command he was ordered to be sent into exile with his wife and children, Arian impiety planned to separate the little sons from their parents, so that through their love it might break down the parents' courage as well. The children, those tender pledges, were taken from them. When he wanted to weep, his wife's authority rebuked him, and his tears dried at once at their very source. For his wife said: "Liberatus, are you going to lose your soul for your sons' sake? Count them as never born, for Christ will surely vindicate them himself. Do you not see them crying out and saying, 'We are Christians'?"

But what this woman did in the sight of the judges must not be passed over in silence. She and her husband were held in prison, though separately, so that they could not see each other at all. A message was sent to the woman: "Give up your obstinacy now. Look, your husband has obeyed the king's command and has become our Christian." She replied: "Let me see him, and I too will do what God wills." So she was brought out of prison and found her husband standing in chains before the tribunal with a great crowd. Believing what the enemies had invented, she grabbed the edges of his clothing nearest his throat and, in sight of all, began to choke him, saying: "Lost and reprobate man, unworthy of God's grace and mercy, why did you choose to glory for a little while and perish forever? What good will gold do you, or silver? Will they free you from the furnace of hell?" And she said many other things. Her husband answered her: "What is the matter with you, woman? What are you imagining, or what can you have heard about me? In the name of Christ I remain a Catholic, and I can never lose what I hold." Then the heretics, aware of their lie and exposed, could not gloss over their deceit at all.

(V, 15) Since we have spoken briefly above about the violence of their savagery: many people, men and women, fearing it, shut themselves away, some in caves, others in deserted places, without anyone knowing. There, with no food to sustain them, overcome by hunger or cold, they breathed out a broken and contrite spirit, yet amid these afflictions they carried with them the security of an unbroken faith. Thus Cresconius, a presbyter of the city of Mizeita, was found in a cave on Mount Ziquensis, set free, his body already decaying.

(V, 16) And since we have already spoken of the holy Habetdeum: he then set out for Carthage and resolved to approach the wicked king, so as to make plain to men as well his conscience, which the Trinity had always held as an intimate and a friend; and Antony could not hold him back, because of his own shame. He presented the most impious king with a petition in words to this effect: "What, I ask, do you still have against men already cast out? Why do you fight every day against those you have banished into exile? You have taken our property and robbed us of churches, homeland and homes; only the soul is left, and this you strive to take captive. O the times, O the morals! The whole world understands this, and the persecutor himself sees it. If what you hold is called a faith, why do you harass the members of the true faith with such persecutions? What business have you with our exile, what business with those who are destitute in this world, whose life is always in Christ? At least let those whom you have cast out from the sight of all peoples be allowed to enjoy the company of the wild beasts."

When the bishop of God had said these and similar things, the criminal tyrant is reported to have sent him this reply: "Go to our bishops and do what they tell you, for they are known to have full authority in this matter." But not even this could call Antony back from his madness, since he knew that by it he could greatly please the impious king. Bishop Habetdeum, however, rejoicing in the good of his conscience, chose to return to his place of exile.

(V, 17) At that time an incredible famine arose and began to lay waste all Africa in one common devastation. No rain fell then; not a single drop came down from the sky. Nor was this without cause; it was by the true and just judgment of God, so that where, under the Arian persecutors, the water of a muddy pool had boiled with fire and sulphur, the rain of heavenly mercy, which had always been abundant, should be withheld. The whole face of the earth was left sallow. The vine was not clothed in summer, shaded with its leafy shoots; the sown fields did not turn the face of the earth green; the olive, always green and full of pleasant leaves, lacked the covering that was its usual beauty; the young fruit trees, though wedded to the earth, had put forth no flower buds to bear fruit afterwards, as they usually do.

Everything was utterly sad and gloomy, and a disaster like a plague had thrown all Africa into confusion. The earth had brought forth no green sprouting grass at all, either for men or for beasts. The beds of rivers that once ran with headlong force had long since dried up, and the rippling veins of the springs, their constant flow cut off, had dried up as well. Sheep and cattle, all of them, and besides them the beasts of the field and the wild animals of the woods, were consumed by hunger and nowhere to be seen at all. And if somewhere grassy turf, still moist in a valley, had begun to put forth the colour of new hay, pale rather than green, at once a burning, fiery wind came and scorched it all dry, for a dust storm under the parched sky, baking everything, had clouded every place.

No trade was carried on at that time. No plough drawn by bullocks cut and turned a single clod of earth, for there were no oxen to hand and no homesteads had survived at all. Part of the peasants' labour force had perished, and whatever part survived was soon seeking burial. And since, under the pressure of famine, neither did trade go on as usual, as we have said, nor were the fields given their due cultivation, throngs that were at the same time walking corpses—young men, old men, youths and maidens, boys and even little girls—spread everywhere, wherever they could and however they could, wandering round the towns, villages and every city. For they had turned into a crooked bow and provoked God at the water of contradiction; they suffered hunger like dogs, not to eat bread, but to feel the hostility of the One whom they had

denied: the Trinity. Some scattered through the fields, others sought the hidden places of the woods, hunting for old roots of plants or other refuse. Some, as they tried to leave their houses, collapsed on the very threshold and fell in heaps, overcome by hunger. The streets and paths were filled with corpses, and the stench of the dead killed the living who walked there on every side. Every day and everywhere the dead and dying lay about, and there was no strength left to offer them the mercy of burial; for the living were not enough to bury them, since hunger held sway and they too would die soon after. People longed to sell their own freedom and their children's into perpetual slavery, and could find no buyer. Mountains and hills, city squares, roads and paths had everywhere become one tomb for all whom hunger, feeding on them, had denied their food.

The Vandals themselves, whom first the possession of Africa and then the frequent spoils of many provinces had made rich, were tormented by even greater want; and the prouder they seemed with their crowds of slaves, the more they wasted away, worn out by the torment of hunger. No one kept his son, no one his wife, no one his own slave; each went out, not where he wished but where he was able, and either died at once or never came back at all.

The unhappy multitude was driven to gather in the city of Carthage itself. As these still-breathing corpses streamed there in crowds, the king saw the slaughter of deaths that would follow, and at once ordered all of them driven out of the city, so that the contagion of the dying should not prepare a common tomb for his army too. He therefore commanded each to be sent back to his own province and home; but there were none to return, since each of them bore his burial in his face. And perhaps the damnation of the rebaptized proved all the greater for this reason: the Arians had promised them a continuation of this present life, and that did not come about, and the second death followed the first. Famine, laying waste, so fully claimed dominion for itself that some places, once very populous, now lie in deep silence, their inhabitants gone, only their walls standing.

(V, 18) But why do I go on lingering over what I cannot describe? If they were alive now and were permitted to speak of such things, the river of Cicero's eloquence would run dry and Sallust would be left utterly tongueless. To pass over outsiders unworthy of so great a subject: if Eusebius of Caesarea, who was equal to such a work, were to rise again, or his translator Rufinus, adorned with Greek eloquence and Latin flowers—why say more?—not Ambrose, not Jerome, not even our own Augustine would be equal to it. Hear this, all you peoples; give ear, all who dwell in the world, both earthborn and sons of men, rich and poor together.

Some of you love the barbarians and sometimes praise them, to your own condemnation: consider the name and understand their character. Could they be called by any other proper name than barbarians, a word that carries the sense of ferocity, cruelty and terror? However many gifts you lavish on them, however much deference you use to soothe them, they know nothing but envy of the Romans. As far as their will goes, they always desire to darken the splendour and race of the Roman name; they want no Roman at all to live. Where they are still known to spare their subjects, they spare them in order to use them as slaves; for they have never loved any Roman.

If barbarian ferocity was trying to debate the faith with us, and if the Arian heresy debated reasonably—but when has it ever held to reason, since it separates God the Son, the Saviour, from God the Father?—why did they act with tricks and slanders, and like a stormy wind try to overturn everything with the tempest of their fury? If an episcopal debate was needed, why gallows, why fires, why hooks and crosses? Why did the serpent brood of the Arians devise against the innocent such kinds of torture as not even Mezentius himself thought up? The lust of fury and the greed of cruelty fought against innocence, to destroy souls and plunder property. If a conference was what they wanted, why the seizure of other people's goods, not only of the priests but of all the laity? But those who were stripped rejoiced and accepted the plundering of their goods with joy.

(V, 19) I beg that every age, every sex and every condition may now be present; I implore that the whole throng of the Catholic name may be present, which is carried in a mother's bosom throughout the whole world, because it alone knows how to offer a brother's affection, having learned from Paul its teacher both to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep.
